docs.title: Algorithm with Numbers
docs.text:
• Here, Complexity refers to bit complexity. i.e., number of operations we have to do on a bit (not a number as a whole)
Operation Complexity Addition O(n) Subtraction O(n) Multiplication O(\(n^2\)) Division O(\(n^2\)) Modular Exponentiation O(\(n^3\)) GCD (Euclid) O(\(n^3\)) Modular Division O(\(n^3\)) #### Addition --- - Result of two n bits numbers result in a sum of at most n + 1 bits - Complexity is O(n) #### Subtraction --- - Same as Addition #### Multiplication --- 
def multiply(x, y):
    if y == 0: # O(n) for comparing each bit with 0
        return 0 # O(1)
    z = multiply(x, floor(y / 2)) # O(1)
    if y is even: # O(1) only the last bit has to be checked
        return 2z # O(n) -> n bit shift
    else: 
        return x + 2z # O(n) -> n bit shift + n bit addition
  • Shift operation requires O(n) time
  • Odd or even check takes only O(1) time (only the last bit has to be checked)
  • Number of recursive calls:
  • log(y) = log(2^n) = n
  • Cost of each recursive calls: O(n) time (maximum of O(1) and O(n))
  • So total cost = O(\(n^2\))

[!example] 18 * 15

Recursive Calls Return Values 18, 15 126*2 + 18 = 270 18, 7 54*2 + 18 = 126 18, 3 18*2 + 18 = 54 18, 1 0*2 + 18 = 18 18, 0 0 #### Division --- 
def divide(x, y):
    if x == 0: # O(n) for comparing each bit with 0
        return (0, 0) # O(1)
    q, r = divide(floor(x / 2), y) # O(1)
    q = 2q # O(n) shift
    r = 2r # O(n) shift
    if x is odd: # O(1) last bit check
        r = r + 1 # O(n) addition
    if r >= y: # O(n) comparison
        r = r - y # O(n) subtraction
        q = q + 1 # O(n) addition
    return (q, r)
  • Number of recursive calls:
  • log(x) = log(2^n) = n
  • Each recursive calls takes O(n) time (maximum of O(1) and O(n))
  • Therefore, total time complexity is O(\(n^2\))

[!example] 113 / 5

Recursive Calls Return Values 113, 5 (11*2, 1*2) = (22, 2) 56, 5 (2*5, 2*3) = (10, 6) = (11, 1) 28, 5 (2*2, 4*2) = (4, 8) = (5, 3) 14, 5 (1*2, 2*2) = (2, 4) 7, 5 (0*2, 2*3 + 1) = (0, 7) = (1, 2) 3, 5 (0*2, 2*1 + 1) = (0, 3) 1, 5 (0*2, 2*0 + 1) = (0, 1) 0, 5 (0, 0) #### Modular Exponentiation --- - Given X, Y and N, we need to find \(X^Y (mod N)\) 
def modexp(x, y, N):
    if y == 0: # O(n) each bit compared to 0
        return 1 # O(1)
    z = modexp(x, floor(y / 2), N) # O(1)
    if y is even: # O(1) last bit compared
        return z^2 mod N # O(n^2) for squaring and O(n^2) for taking modulus by division
    else 
        return x * z^2 mod N # O(n^2) for squaring, O(n^2) for multiplication and O(n^2) for taking modulus by division

[!example] \(20^{17} mod 15\)

Recursive Calls Return Values 20, 17, 15 \(20 * 10^2 mod 15\) = 5 20, 8, 15 \(10^2 mod 15\) = 10 20, 4, 15 \(10^2 mod 15\) = 10 20, 2, 15 \(5^2 mod 15\) = 10 20, 1, 15 \(20 * 1^2 mod 15\) = 5 20, 0, 15 1 - Total number of recursive calls: - log(y) = log(2^n) = n - Each recursive call takes \(O(n^2)\) time - Therefore, total time = \(O(n^3)\)

docs.title: Euclid's Algorithm (Finding GCD)
docs.text:
• We need to find the GCD of two numbers
  • According to Algorithm (considering a >= b)
  • gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)
def gcd(a, b):
    if b == 0: # O(n) n bit comparison with 0 
        return a # O(1)
    return gcd(b, a mod b) # O(n^2) modulus requires O(n^2) division
  • Each recursive call required \(O(n^2)\) time

[!quote] Lemma If a >= b, then a mod b < a / 2

Proof: Either b <= a / 2 or b > a / 2. If b <= a / 2, a mod b will always be less than b => a mod b < b. And we have b <= a / 2 => a mod b < b <= a / 2 => a mod b < a / 2 If b > a / 2, then we can have only one b inside a and the remaining will be obviously less than a / 2 since b has already taken a / 2.

From the above lemma, we can see that, at each step the number will be reduced by at least half. i.e., the length of the number reduces by at least 1 bit in every recursive call. So, after maximum 2n recursive calls, we will reach the base case. So at maximum there will be O(n) recursive calls. Therefore the total complexity is \(O(n^3)\)

[!quote] Proof We need to prove gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) i.e., gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, r) where r = a mod b - Suppose d|a and d|b - a = bq + r - => r = a - bq - Since d divides both a and b, it divides a and bq => it divides r

So, any common divisor of (a, b) also divides (b, r) - Now, d|b and d|r - a = bq + r - Since d|b and d|r, d divides bq and d divides r => d divides a

So, any common divisor of (b, r) also divides (a, b) i.e., common divisors of (a, b) = common divisors (b, r) So their gcd is also the same => gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, r)

[!info] Worst case for Euclid's Algorithm happens when the numbers are consecutive Fibonacci numbers

docs.title: Extended Euclid's Algorithm
docs.text:
[!quote] Lemma if d divides a and b and d = ax + by for some integer x and y then d = gcd(a, b)

Proof: - Since d divides a and b, it is a common divisor. So it cannot exceed the greatest common divisor of a and b. i.e, d <= gcd(a, b) - Since, gcd divides a and b, it divides any linear combination of a and b, i.e., gcd divides ax + by. - => gcd <= ax + by - => gcd <= d - => gcd <= d and gcd >= d => gcd = d

  • Extended Euclid's Algorithm gives us both the gcd (d) as well as x and y such that d = gcd(a, b) = ax + by
def extended_euclid_algo(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return (a, 1, 0)
    else:
        (d, x, y) = extended_euclid_algo(b, a mod b)
        return (d, y, x - floor(a / b) * y)

[!example] (21, 18)

Recursive Calls Return Value 21, 18 (3, 1, 0 - floor(21 / 18) * 1) = (3, 1, -1) 18, 3 (3, 0, 1 - floor(21 / 18) * 0) = (3, 0, 1) 3, 0 (3, 1, 0)

[!quote] Correctness of proof We know, \(a = \left \lfloor{\frac{a}{b}}\right \rfloor b + a mod b\) And, \(d = gcd(b, a mod b) \implies d = x'b + y'amodb\) => \(d = x'b + y'\{a - \left \lfloor{\frac{a}{b}}\right \rfloor b\}\)

docs.title: Modular Division
docs.text:
• We say x is the multiplicative inverse of a modulo N if ax ≡ 1 mod N

[!important] For any a mod N , a has a multiplicative inverse modulo N if and only if it is relatively prime to N . When this inverse exists, it can be found in time \(O(n^3)\) by running the extended Euclid algorithm.

  • i.e., when we run an extended-euclid algorithm, we find x and y such that, ax + by = gcd(a, N)
  • but here, gcd(a, N) = 1
  • => ax + Ny = 1
  • => ax mod N + Ny mod N = 1 mod N
  • => ax mod N + 0 = 1 mod N
  • => ax mod N = 1 mod N
  • => ax ≡ 1 mod N
  • => \(a^{-1} = x\)

docs.title: Fibonacci Numbers
docs.text:
• Finding Fibonacci numbers using DP takes O(n) time.
  • But if we use matrices, we can find it in O(logN) number of matrix multiplications
\[ \begin{pmatrix} F_{2}\\ F_{1}\\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0\\ \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} F_{1}\\ F_{0}\\ \end{pmatrix} $$ - Using this matrix, we can find F2 and F1 - By doing this again and again $$ \begin{pmatrix} F_{k+1}\\ F_{k}\\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0\\ \end{pmatrix}^{k} \begin{pmatrix} F_{1}\\ F_{0}\\ \end{pmatrix} $$ - This does not required k matrix multiplications - This requires only log k number of matrix multiplications - Therefore by this method, we can efficiently find Fibonacci numbers $$ \begin{array}{l} z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \\[6pt] \text{if $k$ is even:} \\ \quad \text{return } z^2 \\[6pt] \text{else:} \\ \quad \text{return } \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \cdot z^2 \end{array} \]

docs.title: Prime Number Theorem
docs.text: \(\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} {\frac{\pi_n}{\frac{n}{lnn}} = 1}\) \(\text{for very large n: } \pi_n \approx \frac{n}{lnn}\) - roughly every ln(n)-th number near n is prime

docs.title: Primality Test
docs.text:
• First approach is to divide n by 1 to \(\sqrt{n}\). If none of the remainders are 0, then n is prime. (we can avoid even integers > 2)
  • But, it will take \(O(\sqrt{n})\) time = \(O(n^{1/2}) = O(2^N/2) = O(2^{N - 1})\) which is exponential
  • But this method gives us unnecessary information(We just need to check if the number is prime or not, but this method tells us the factors of the number, which is unnecessary)
  • The best method to use is Pseudo Primality Testing

docs.title: Pseudo Primality Testing
docs.text:
• This is a method for primality testing that "almost works". In fact, is good enough for many practical applications
  • The idea is:
    • if n is prime, then Zn+ = Zn*
    • Because, if n is prime, then all the numbers between 1 and n will be co-prime to n.
  • We use Fermat's Little Theorem here
  • So we take a number "a" which is less than n
  • Find \(a^{p-1} \text{ mod p}\). If it is 1, then the n is prime, otherwise n is composite
  • Modular exponentiation takes only \(O(n^3)\) time. Therefore the complexity of this method is \(O(n^3)\)
  • But this method can give false positives
    • i.e., If a number is prime, then the algorithm would always say it is prime
    • But is the number is composite, then it is not guaranteed that it will say it is composite
    • In such cases, we need to take multiple values of a to check (If the number is prime, then for all a, the result will be 1)
    • But in that case also, there are specific numbers called Carmicheal's numbers which gives wrong result(is composite but will give 1 for all values of 1)

[!tip] Carmicheal Numbers examples: 561

docs.title: Multiplication of Complex Numbers
docs.text: $\((a + bi) * (c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i\)$ - This contains 4 multiplications - Multiplication is more expensive than addition, So we try to reduce the number of multiplications (which may increase the number of additions) $$ \begin{aligned} P_1 &= ac \ P_2 &= bd \ P_3 &= (a + b)(c + d) \ \therefore \text{Real Part} &= P_1 - P_2 \ \text{Imaginary Part} &= P_3 - P_1 - P_2 \end{aligned} $$ - By this method, we reduce the number of multiplications from 4 to 3. But the number of additions increased from 2 to 5, which is not much expensive compared to multiplications

docs.title: Multiplication of 2 Numbers
docs.text:
• Multiplication of two numbers in naive method results in \(O(n^2)\) time
  • Multiplication of two numbers can also be done efficiently by divide and conquer. In each step we split the number in middle. And we multiply them only if the numbers get reduced to one bit (In practical computers, there is no need to divide them till 1 bit, most of the computers can handle 16-bit or 32-bit multiplications as a single operation) $$ \begin{aligned} X &= 2^{n/2}X_L + X_R \ Y &= 2^{n/2}Y_L + Y_R \ \end{aligned} $$
  • The power of 2, shifts the left part n/2 positions and then the right part is added to it resulting in the original number

docs.title: Naive method
docs.text: $$ \begin{aligned} XY &= (2^{n/2}X_L + X_R) * (2^{n/2}Y_L + Y_R) \ &= 2^nX_LY_L + (X_RY_L + X_LY_R)\cdot 2^{n/2} + X_RY_R \ \end{aligned} $$ - This needs 4 multiplications - And each time we are splitting the number in half - => T(n) = 4T(n / 2) + O(n) - => T(n) = \(O(n^2)\)

docs.title: Better method
docs.text:
• Here we need to compute \(X_RY_L + X_LY_R\) which can be rewritten as: $$ \begin{aligned} X_RY_L + X_LY_R &= (X_L + X_R)\cdot(Y_L + Y_R) - X_LY_L - X_RY_R \ \end{aligned} $$
  • This looks like we have increased the number of multiplications from 2 to 3, but we can see that, the \(X_LY_L\) term and \(X_RY_R\) term we have already computed. Which means, we reduced the number of multiplications from a total of 4 to 3 $$ \begin{aligned} P_1 &= X_LY_L \ P_2 &= X_RY_R \ P_3 &= (X_L + X_R)(Y_L + Y_R) \ X\cdot Y &= 2^nP_1 + 2^{n/2}(P_3 - P_2 - P_1) + P_2 \ \end{aligned} $$
  • This way we reduced the number of multiplications from 4 to 3, Also since we are splitting the number is half, the number of bits being multiplied at a time is also reduced
def multiply(x, y):
    if n == 1:
        return x * y
    X_L = left half of x
    X_R = right half of x
    Y_L = left half of y
    Y_R = right half of Y

    P_1 = multiply(X_L, Y_L)
    P_2 = multiply(X_R, Y_R)
    P_3 = multiply(X_L + X_R, Y_L + Y_R)

    return 2^n * P_1 + 2^(n/2) * (P_3 - P_2 - P_1) + P_2
  • Since, there are 3 multiplications and each at each step we are splitting the number in halves
  • => T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n)
  • => T(n) = \(O(n^{\log_{2}(3)}) = O(n^{1.585})\)
  • Which is better than \(O(n^2)\)

[!question] Find the k-th smallest element in an unsorted Array

docs.title: Naive Solution
docs.text:
• To solve the k-th smallest element solution, first approach would be sorting and taking the k-th element from the sorted array
  • But this will take O(nlogn) time since we need to sort the array

docs.title: Quick Select
docs.text:
• A better way of solving the above question is using Quick select
  • The concept of quick select is:
    • We pick a pivot from the array and partition the array so that
      • All elements in the left is smaller than the pivot
      • All elements in the right is greater than the pivot
    • After partition:
      • If the index of pivot == k, then pivot is the answer
      • If the index of pivot < k, recursively search the right part
      • If the index of pivot > k, recursively search the left part
  • Partioning the array takes O(n) time
  • Best time complexity: O(n)
  • Worst time complexity: \(O(n^2)\) => If the pivot we take always lies in the starting or ending of the array after partitioning, then it will take \(O(n^2)\) time
def quick_select(arr, left, right, k):
    if left == right:
        return arr[left]

    pivotIndex = partition(arr, left, right)

    if pivotIndex == k:
        return arr[pivotIndex]
    elif k < length:
        return quick_select(arr, left, pivotIndex - 1, k)
    else:
        return quick_select(arr, pivotIndex + 1, right, k)

def partition(arr, left, right):
    pivot = arr[right]
    i = left

    for j in range(left, right):
        if arr[j] <= pivot:
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
            i += 1
    arr[i], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[i]
    return i

docs.title: Median of Median's Approach
docs.text:
• The problem with the previous QuickSelect example was the choosing of pivot. If we choose wrong pivot all the time, we get quadratic time, where as if we choose the right pivot, we get the answer in linear time.
  • Instead of picking a pivot randomly (like QuickSelect does), we carefully pick a "good pivot" that ensures the array shrinks fast enough
  • Steps:
    • Divide the array into groups of 5 each (last group may contain fewer elements)
    • Find the median of each group (constant time, since each group contains at max 5 elements)
    • Recursively find the median of these medians -> this will be our pivot
    • Partition the array around this pivot (like QuickSelect)
    • Depending on where the pivot lands:
      • if pivot's position == k: return pivot
      • if pivot's position < k: recurse right
      • else: recurse left

[!question] Why is this efficient? - In each group of 5, at least 3 elements will be >= group median and at least 3 elements will be <= group median - Since we take the median of these medians, at least half of the medians are >= pivot - This means at least 30% of all elements are >= pivot and at least 30% <= pivot - So the pivot is never too skewed -> We remove at least 30% of the elements in each partition

[!important] Complexity Analysis - Step 1: Splitting the array into groups of 5: O(n) - Step 2: Finding the median of each group: O(n) (constant time per group) - Step 2: Recursively find the medians: T(n/5) - Step 3: Partition around pivot: O(n) - Step 4: Recurse into at most 70% of the array: T(7n/10)

So, T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n) => T(n) <= T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + dn for some d > 0 We assume T(n) <= cn for some constant c and try to prove it by induction => \(T(n) \le c\frac{n}{5} + c\frac{7n}{10} + dn\) => \(T(n) \le cn(\frac{1}{5} + \frac{7}{10} + \frac{d}{c})\) => \(T(n) \le cn(\frac{2}{10} + \frac{7}{10} + \frac{d}{c})\) => \(T(n) \le cn(\frac{9}{10} + \frac{d}{c})\) Take c >= 10d => \(T(n) \le cn(\frac{9}{10} + \frac{1}{10})\) => \(T(n) \le cn\frac{10}{10}\) => \(T(n) \le cn\) => taking appropriate value for d gives as T(n) = O(n)

Base case: - T(5) <= 10 i.e., T(n) <= 5c for all c >= 2 Time complexity can be proved using Extended Masters Theorem also

docs.title: Maximum sub-array sum
docs.text: Given an array of integers (can contain positives and negatives), find the contiguous sub-array with the maximum sum

docs.title: Brute-force method
docs.text:
• Find all sub-arrays of the given array
  • Find the maximum sum among the sub-arrays
  • Generating all sub-arrays need \(O(n^3)\) time
  • Therefore complexity is \(O(n^3)\)

docs.title: Divide and conquer approach
docs.text:
• We split the array into two equal halves
  • The maximum sub array can lie in the following three possible places
    • Entirely in the left sub-array
    • Entirely in the right sub-array
    • Partly in the left and partly in the right sub-array
  • maxSubArraySum(arr, l, r) = max(maxSubArraySum(arr, l, mid), maxSubArraySum(arr, mid + 1, r), maxCrossingSum(arr, l, mid, r))

Steps: - Base case: If the array has only one element: return that element - Divide: Find the middle index "mid". - Conquer: Recursively find the maximum sub-array sum in the left half and right half - Combine: Find the maximum sub-array sum crossing the middle - Compute maximum sum starting from mid and going left - Compute maximum sum starting from mid + 1 and going right - Add them to get the crossing sum - Finally, take the maximum among the three

def maxSubArraySum(arr, l, r):
    if l == r:
        return arr[l]

    mid = (l + r) // 2

    left_sum = maxSubArraySum(arr, l, mid)
    right_sum = maxSubArraySum(arr, mid + 1, r)
    cross_sum = maxCrossingSum(arr, l, mid, r)

    return max(left_sum, right_sum, cross_sum)

def maxCrossingSum(arr, l, mid, r):
    sum = 0
    left_max = -inf
    for i = mid downTo 1:
        sum += arr[i]
        left_max = max(left_max, sum)

    sum = 0
    right_max = -inf
    for i = mid + 2 upto r:
        sum += arr[i]
        right_max = max(right_max, max)

    return left_max + right_max

[!info] Time Complexity - T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) - 2 T(n/2) comes from the recursion for left and right sub arrays - O(n) comes is for calculating the maximum crossing sum - From the recurrence, we get T(n) = O(nlogn) - Each level of recursion takes O(n) time for finding max crossing sum - There is logn number of recursive calls - Therefore, total time complexity is O(nlogn)

[!tip] Divide and conquer is giving O(nlogn) time whereas kadane's algorithm gives result in O(n) time

docs.title: Counting Inversions
docs.text:
Given an array, we want to count the number of inversions An inversion is a pair of indices (i, j) such that i < j and arr[i] > arr[j]

[!example] [2, 4, 1, 3, 5] Inversions: - (2, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3) => (Here the numbers are not indices, they are the values) - Therefore, Total = 3 inversions

docs.title: Brute force solution
docs.text:
• Compare every pair of (i, j)
  • If arr[i] > arr[j] and i < j, increment count
  • Since we need to check all the possible pairs of (i, j), it takes \(O(n^2)\) time
def countInverse(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    count = 0
    for i = 0 to n - 2:
        for j = i + 1 to n - 1:
            if arr[i] > arr[j]:
                count += 1
    return count

docs.title: Divide and conquer Solution
docs.text:
• We divide the array into left and right half
  • Inversion can come in three types:
    • Both indices in left half
    • Both indices in right half
    • One index in left and other in right half
def countInversions(arr, l, r):
    if l >= r:
        return 0

    mid = (l + r) // 2

    left_inv = countInversions(arr, l, mid)
    right_inv = countInversions(arr, mid + 1, r)
    cross_inv = mergeAndCount(arr, l, mid, r)

    return left_inv + right_inv + cross_inv

def mergeAndCount(arr, l, mid, r):
    left = arr[l..mid]
    right = arr[mid + 1..r]
    i = 0
    j = 0
    k = 1
    inv_count = 0

    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            arr[k] = left[i]
            i += 1
        else:
            arr[k] = right[j]
            j += 1
            inv_count += (length(left) - i)
        k += 1

    while i < len(left): 
        arr[k] = left[i]
        i += 1
        k += 1
    while j < len(right):
        arr[k] = right[j]
        j += 1
        k += 1

    return inv_count
  • The concept is: when we mergeAndCount, we merge the array in sorted manner so that, when we compare an element in left with an element in right and finds that it is an inversion, then all the elements in the left array after that number will be inversions
  • example:
  • left = [2, 4], right = [1, 3, 5]
  • since (2, 1) is an inversion (4, 1) will also be an inversion, which is not needed to be checked since the arrays will be sorted.
  • T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
  • => T(n) = O(nlogn)

docs.title: Lower bounds
docs.text: Uses of lower bounds: - Helps in design algorithms - Rules out many algorithms

docs.title: Comparison Model
docs.text:
• Only operation allowed is comparison
  • Result of operation is "yes" or "no"

docs.title: Decision Tree
docs.text:
• Binary tree
  • Internal nodes are single comparison
  • Leaf nodes are possible outcomes

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
• For an input array of n elements, there are n! possible solutions

[!example] If the array is: [a1, a2, a3] Then, possible solutions include - [a1, a2, a3] - [a1, a3, a2] - [a2, a1, a3] - [a2, a3, a1] - [a3, a1, a2] - [a3, a2, a1] - => For 3 element array, there are 6 possibilities => 3!

- Number of possible solutions = n! - Numbers of leafs >= n! - height = Ω(log(n!)) - = Ω(log(n) + log(n - 1) + log(n - 1) + ... + log(2) + log(1)) - By sterling approximation (log(n!) > nlogn - n) - => height = Ω(nlogn)

docs.title: Naive solution
docs.text: • Sort the array and take the last element

docs.title: Optimized Approach
docs.text:
• Using Decision Tree
  • We take an array A which contains the list of possible results
  • At each internal node, we compare two values say a and b, If a < b is true, then we remove a from A. If a < b is false, then we remove b from A
  • At each level, we eliminate one element from the result array
  • For an array of n elements, we need n - 1 comparisons => Height of tree is n - 1 = Ω(n)

docs.title: Finding both minimum and maximum together in an array
First approach
docs.text:
def findMinMax(arr):
    min = max = arr[0]
    for num in arr:
        if num < min:
            min = num
        elif num > max:
            max = num

    return (min, max)
  • The problem here is, there is a loop running n - 1 times and in each loop we do 2 comparisons. Therefore we have minimum 2n - 2 comparisons.
  • Asymptotically its Ω(n). But we can reduce the number of comparisons

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
• We keep a MIN array and MAX array each containing all the elements of the input array
  • We take pairs of consecutive numbers a and b from the array.
  • Then compare the two numbers
  • If a < b:
    • then, a will never be the maximum in the array
    • So, pop out a from MAX
    • Also, b will never be the minimum in the array
    • So, pop out b from MIN
  • If a > b:
    • then a will never be the minimum in the array
    • So, pop out a from MIN
    • Also, b will never be the maximum in the array
    • So, pop out b from MAX
  • Do this repeatedly.
  • After all the pairs are compared, the MIN and MAX arrays will have n/2 elements each.
  • But till now we have done n/2 comparisons only.
  • From the MIN array, now we can find the minimum by the first approach with n/2 - 1 comparisons
  • Also, from the MAX array, we can find the maximum by the first approach with n/2 - 1 comparisons
  • In this way, we can find the result in n/2 + (n/2 - 1) + (n/2 - 1) comparisons
  • => 3n/2 - 2 comparisons which is less than 2n - 2
def findMinMax(arr, n):
    MIN[n/2]
    MAX[n/2]
    k = 0

    for i = 0 to n - 1 step 2:
        if arr[i] < arr[i+1]:
            MIN[k] = arr[i]
            MAX[k] = arr[i+1]
        else:
            MIN[k] = arr[i+1]
            MAX[k] = arr[i]
        k += 1

    min_val = MIN[0]
    for num in MIN:
        if num < min_val:
            min_val = num

    max_val = MAX[0]
    for num in MAX:
        if num > max_val:
            max_val = num

    return (min_val, max_val)

docs.title: Adversary Argument Approach
docs.text:
• Algorithm can query the adversary.
  • Adversary need not give the correct answers, but the answers should agree each other. i.e., previous answer should not contradict the next answer.
  • We count the number of queries asked as a measure of time complexity
  • Algorithm can asks only yes or no questions
  • When the adversary has two options to answer, it will always answer the one which will require more steps to reach the leaf (find the solution)
  • When algorithm has two options to asks, it will ask the query which will result in reaching the leaf node (finding the solution) in least steps

docs.title: Modular Arithmetics
docs.text:
• (x ≡ y) mod N means N divides (x - y)
  • Another interpretation is that modular arithmetic deals with all the integers, but divides them into N equivalence classes, each of the form {i + kN : k ∈ Z} for some i between 0 and N − 1. For example, there are three equivalence classes modulo 3

[!example] · · · −9 −6 −3 0 3 6 9 · · · · · · −8 −5 −2 1 4 7 10 · · · · · · −7 −4 −1 2 5 8 11 · · ·

  • Any member of an equivalence class is substitutable for any other; when viewed modulo 3, the numbers 5 and 11 are no different. Under such substitutions, addition and multiplication remain well-defined.

[!important] Substitution Rule if x ≡ x' (mod N) and y ≡ y' (mod N), then x + y ≡ x' + y' (mod N) and xy ≡ x'y' (mod N)

[!example] \(2^{345} \equiv (2^5)^{69} \equiv 32^{69} \equiv 1^{69} \equiv 1 (mod 31)\)

[!important] Associativity x + (y + z) ≡ (x + y) + z (mod N) Commutativity xy ≡ yx (mod N) Distributivity x(y + z) ≡ xy + xz (mod N)

docs.title: \(Z_n\)
docs.text:
• this is the set of equivalence classes represented by numbers in range 0 to n - 1
  • for simplicity, its just 0 -> n - 1 \(Z_n = \{[a]_n : a \in {0, ..., n - 1} \}\) \(Z_n = \{[0]_n, [1]_n, ..., [n - 1]_n\}\)
  • this is often written as {0, 1, 2, ..., n - 1}

docs.title: \(Z_n^+\)
docs.text:
• this is the set \(Z_n\) excluding 0 \(Z_n^+ = \{[1]_n, ..., [n - 1]_n\} = Z_n - \{0\}\)
  • this is often written as {1, 2, 3, ..., n - 1}

docs.title: \([a]_n\)
docs.text: • this is the set of numbers in the equivalence class of a, i.e., numbers whose modulus N will be same as a mod N \([a]_n = \{b \in Z | b \equiv a mod N \}\) \([2]_5 = \{..., -8, -3, 2, 7, 12, ...\}\)

docs.title: \(Z_n^*\)
docs.text: • this is the set of numbers which are co-prime to n and is less than n \(Z^*_n = \{[a]_n \in Z_n | gcd (a, n) = 1\}\) \(Z^*_8 = \{1, 3, 5, 7\} \text{= coprimes of 8 from 1 to 8}\)

docs.title: \(\pi_n\)
docs.text: • this is the number of primes less than or equal to n \(\pi_n = \text{number of primes} \le n\)

docs.title: Time Complexity Analysis
docs.text:
• Big-O Notation (O): Asymptotic Upper Bound
    • f(n) = O(g(n)) means f(n) grows no faster than g(n).
    • Formal Definition: There exist constants c > 0 and n₀ > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c * g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
    • Example: 3n² + 5n + 10 = O(n²).
  • Big-Omega Notation (Ω): Asymptotic Lower Bound
    • f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f(n) grows at least as fast as g(n).
    • Formal Definition: There exist constants c > 0 and n₀ > 0 such that 0 ≤ c * g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
    • Example: 3n² + 5n + 10 = Ω(n²).
  • Big-Theta Notation (Θ): Asymptotic Tight Bound
    • f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means f(n) grows at the same rate as g(n).
    • Formal Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) and f(n) = Ω(g(n)).
    • Example: 3n² + 5n + 10 = Θ(n²).

docs.title: Fermat's Little Theorem
docs.text: • If p is a prime number, then for all integer a < p, $$ a^{p-1} = 1 \text{ mod p} $$

docs.title: Masters Theorem
docs.text: \[ \begin{aligned} \text{For } T(n) &= aT(n/b) + O(n^k) \\ \text{Find } x &= log_b{a} \\ \text{If } x \lt k: T(n) &= O(n^k) \\ \text{If } x \gt k: T(n) &= O(n^x) \\ \text{If } x = k: T(n) &= O(n^xlog^{k + 1}n) \\ \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Extended Masters Theorem
docs.text:
$$ \begin{aligned} \text{General Form: }\ T(x) &= \sum\limits_{i=1}^k a_iT(b_ix) + g(x) \ \text{where } 0 < b_i &< 1 \ \text{and } a_i &> 0 \ \text{and } g(x) &\text{is the cost outside the recusion(like splitting, merging)} \end{aligned} $$ - Define p such that: $$ \sum\limits_{i=1}^k a_ib_i^p = 1 $$ - Compare g(x) with \(x^p\) - If g(x) grows faster than \(x^p\), then T(x) = O(g(x)) - If \(x^p\) grows faster than g(x), then T(x) = \(x^p\) - If both are asymptotically same, then T(x) = O(\(x^plogx\))

[!example] Quick Sort - T(n) = T(n/4) + T(3n/4) + O(n) - Here, \(a_1 = 1, b_1 = 1/4, a_2 = 1, b_2 = 3/4\) - Solve for p - => \((1)(\frac{1}{4})^p + (1)(\frac{3}{4})^p = 1\) - => p = 1 - Now we compare \(n^p\) and O(n) - i.e., we compare O(n) and O(n) - both are asymptotically same => We take \(T(n) = O(n^plogn)\) - => T(n) = O(nlogn)

[!example] Median of Medians Algorithm - T(n) <= T(7n/10) + T(n/5) + O(n) - Here \(a_1 = 1, b_1 = 7/10, a_2 = 1, b_2 = 1/5\) - Solve for p: - => \((1)(\frac{7}{10})^p + (1)(\frac{1}{5})^p = 1\) - => \(p \approx 0.85\) - Now we compare \(n^p\) and O(n) - i.e., we compare \(O(n^{0.85})\) with O(n) - O(n) grows faster, so we takes O(n) - => T(n) = O(n)

docs.title: 🌱 STEP 2: What is an Approximation Algorithm?
docs.text: It’s just an algorithm that: - Runs in polynomial time - Doesn’t give the exact optimal solution - BUT gives a solution that is provably close to optimal The word provably is super important — we are not guessing; we mathematically guarantee that it won’t be too bad.

docs.title: 🌱 STEP 3: Approximation Ratio (the HEART of this topic)
docs.text: Take a breath — this part is important but we’ll go gently. Let’s denote: - ALG = solution given by our approximation algorithm - OPT = value of the optimal solution (the best possible) Depending on the type of problem:

docs.title: ✔ Minimization (example: Vertex Cover, Set Cover)
docs.text:
Smaller is better The algorithm should satisfy: $\(ALG≤ρ(n)⋅OPT\)$ If ρ(n) = 2, that means:

"The algorithm's answer is at most 2 times the optimal."

docs.title: ✔ Maximization (example: Max-SAT)
docs.text:
Bigger is better Here: $\(ALG≥\frac{1}{ρ(n)}⋅OPT\)$ If ρ(n) = 2, that means:

"The algorithm achieves at least half of the optimal."

The approximation ratio tells you:

How bad the algorithm can be in the worst case.

docs.title: Approximation Algorithm for Vertex Cover
docs.text:
• Select an arbitrary edge e
  • Add the vertices u and v of the edge e to the result
  • Remove e and all the edges from u and v from the graph
  • Repeat until the graph is empty
\[|ALG| \le 2|OPT|\]

docs.title: Approximation Algorithm for Set Cover
docs.text:
• Take the set with most number of uncovered elements
  • Mark the elements in this set as covered
  • Repeat until all elements are covered $$ \begin{aligned} |ALG| &\le H_n|OPT| \ H_n &\approx ln(n) \end{aligned} $$

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
• Let OPT = k, i.e., the optimal solution uses k sets to cover all n elements
  • On average, OPT covers n/k elements per set. (This doesn’t mean every OPT set does this — but on average yes.)
  • At ANY moment while running the greedy algorithm, there are still some uncovered elements left.
  • Let’s say at some step there are t uncovered elements.
  • Since OPT used k sets to cover everything,
  • OPT could cover these t remaining elements with at most k sets.
  • So one of those sets must cover at least t/k elements.
  • Because: If k sets cover t elements, average coverage per set=\(\frac{t}{k}\)
  • There must be one set with ≥ average coverage.
  • OPT has a set covering ≥ t/k uncovered elements
  • Greedy picks the set covering the maximum uncovered elements 👉 So greedy will also cover at least t/k elements.
  • Now look at how t decreases Start with:
  • t = n After picking one set, we cover ≥ n/k elements. Remaining uncovered: $$ \begin{aligned} n_1 &\le n - \frac{n}{k} \ n_1 &\le n(1 - \frac{1}{k}) \ n_2 &\le n_1(1 - \frac{1}{k}) \ n_2 &\le n(1 - \frac{1}{k})^2 \ n_i &\le n(1 - \frac{1}{k})^i \ \text{we need to find for what i }& n_i \text{ becomes } \lt 1 \ (1-\frac{1}{k})^k &\approx \frac{1}{e} \ n(1 - \frac{1}{k})^i &= 1 \ \text{using these,} \ \text{we need kln(n) steps} \ |ALG| &\le kln(n) \ |ALG| &\le ln(n) |OPT| \end{aligned} $$

closestPair(X, Y) {
    n = X.length;

    if (n == 2) return dist(X[1], X[2]);
    if (n == 3) min(dist(X[1], X[2]), dist(X[2], X[3]), dist(X[1], X[3]));

    mid = X[n / 2];

    dl = closestPair(X[1...mid], Y);
    dr = closestPair(X[mid + 1...N], Y);

    S = points in Y whose x-coordinates are in the range of [mid.x - d, mid.x + d];
    for i = 1 to S.length:
        for j = 1 to j = 7:
            d = min(d, dist(S[i], S[i + j]))

    return d;
}

docs.title: Merge Sort
docs.text:
public void mergeSort(int[] arr, int low, int high) {
    if (low < high) {
        int mid = (low + high) / 2;
        mergeSort(arr, low, mid);
        mergeSort(arr, mid + 1, high);

        merge(arr, low, mid, high);
    }
}

public void merge(int[] arr, int low, int mid, int high) {
    int n1 = mid - low + 1;
    int n2 = high - mid;

    int[] left = new int[n1];
    int[] right = new int[n2];

    System.arraycopy(arr, low, left, 0, n1);
    System.arraycopy(arr, mid + 1, right, 0, n2);

    int i = 0, j = 0, k = low;

    while (i < n1 && j < n2) {
        if (left[i] < right[j]) {
            arr[k++] = left[i++];
        } else {
            arr[k++] = right[j++];
        }
    }

    while (i < n1) {
        arr[k++] = left[i++];
    }

    while (j < n2) {
        arr[k++] = right[j++];
    }
}

[!tip] Time Complexity O(nlogn)

docs.title: Quick sort
docs.text:
public void quickSort(int[] arr, int low, int high) {
    if (low < high) {
        int pivot = partition(arr, low, high);

        quickSort(arr, low, pivot - 1);
        quickSort(arr, pivot + 1, high);
    }
}

public int partition(int[] arr, int low, int high) {
    for (int i = low; i < high; i++) {
        if (arr[low] < arr[high]) {
            int temp = arr[i];
            arr[i] = arr[low];
            arr[low] = temp;
            low++;
        }
    }

    int temp = arr[low];
    arr[low] = arr[high];
    arr[high] = temp;

    return low;
}

[!tip] Time Complexity O(nlogn)

docs.title: Strassen's Matrix Multiplication
docs.text:
Base case => 2 * 2 matrix => Calculate the resulting 2 * 2 matrix in constant time divide the matrix into 4 halves and recurse

MM(A, B, n):
    if n == 2:
        do 2 * 2 multiplication of matrices

    C11 = MM(A11, B11, n/2) + MM(A12, B21, n/2)
    C12 = MM(A11, B12, n/2) + MM(A12, B22, n/2)
    C21 = MM(A21, B11, n/2) + MM(A22, B21, n/2)
    C22 = MM(A21, B12, n/2) + MM(A21, B22, n/2)

    return C
  • Here each addition is matrix addition => O(n^2)
  • i.e., total complexity is T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n^2) => O(n^3)
  • Strassen optimized the number of multiplications from 8 to 7 resulting in
    • T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2) => O(n^2.81)

public int maxSubarraySum(int[] arr) {
    return solve(arr, 0, arr.length - 1);
}

public int solve(int[] arr, int low, int high) {
    if (low == high) return arr[low];

    int mid = (low + high) / 2;
    int left = solve(arr, low, mid);
    int right = solve(arr, mid + 1, high);
    int middle = computeMiddle(arr, low, mid, high);

    return Math.max(left, Math.max(right, middle));
}

public int computerMiddle(int[] arr, int low, int mid, int high) {
    int leftBest = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    int sum = 0;

    for (int i = mid; i >= low; i--) {
        sum += arr[i];
        leftBest = Math.max(leftBest, sum);
    }

    sum = 0;
    int rightBest = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

    for (int i = mid; i < high; i++) {
        sum += arr[i];
        rightBest = Math.max(rightBest, sum);
    }

    return leftBest + rightBest;
}

static int memo(String s1, String s2, int i, int j, int[][] dp) {
        if (i < 0 || j < 0) return 0;

        if (dp[i][j] != -1) return dp[i][j];

        if (s1.charAt(i) == s2.charAt(j)) {
            return dp[i][j] = memo(s1, s2, i - 1, j - 1, dp) + 1;
        }

        int left = memo(s1, s2, i - 1, j, dp);
        int right = memo(s1, s2, i, j - 1, dp);

        return dp[i][j] = Math.max(left, right);

                if (s1.charAt(i - 1) == s2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                    dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i - 1][j - 1];
                } else {
                    dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
                }
            }
        }

        return dp[m][n];

public int memo(int[] val, int[] wt, int rem, int i, int[][] dp) {
        if (i < 0) return 0;
        if (rem <= 0) return 0;

        if (dp[i][rem] != -1) return dp[i][rem];

        int take = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        if (wt[i] <= rem) {
            take = val[i] + memo(val, wt, rem - wt[i], i - 1, dp);    
        }

        int notTake = memo(val, wt, rem, i - 1, dp);

        return dp[i][rem] = Math.max(take, notTake);
    }

    public int tabulation(int[] val, int[] wt, int W) {
        int n = val.length;
        int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][W + 1];

        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j <= W; j++) {
                int take = 0;
                if (wt[i - 1] <= j) {
                    take = val[i - 1] + dp[i - 1][j - wt[i - 1]];
                }
                int notTake = dp[i - 1][j];

                dp[i][j] = Math.max(take, notTake);
            }
        }

        return dp[n][W];
    }

static Boolean memo(int[] arr, int i, int rem, int[][] dp) {
        if (i < 0 || rem < 0) return rem == 0;
        if (rem == 0) return true;

        if (dp[i][rem] != -1) return dp[i][rem] == 1;

        boolean take = memo(arr, i - 1, rem - arr[i], dp);
        boolean notTake = memo(arr, i - 1, rem, dp);

        dp[i][rem] = take || notTake ? 1 : 0;
        return take || notTake;
    }

    static Boolean tabulation(int[] arr, int sum) {
        int n = arr.length;
        boolean[][] dp = new boolean[n + 1][sum + 1];

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            dp[i][0] = true;
        }

        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            for (int s = 1; s <= sum; s++) {
                boolean notTake = dp[i - 1][s];
                boolean take = false;

                if (s - arr[i - 1] >= 0) take = dp[i - 1][s - arr[i - 1]];

                dp[i][s] = take || notTake;
            }
        }

        return dp[n][sum];
    }

public void floydWarshall(int[][] dist) {
    int n = dist.length;
    int INF = 100_000_000;

    for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                if (dist[i][k] == INF || dist[k][j] == INF) continue;
                dist[i][j] = Math.min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]);
            }
        }
    }
}

public int[] bellmanFord(int V, int[][] edges, int src) {
    int INF = 100_000_000;

    int[] dist = new int[V];
    Arrays.fill(dist, INF);
    dist[src] = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < V - 1; i++) {
        for (int[] edge: edges) {
            int u = edge[0], v = edge[1], weight = edge[2];

            if (dist[u] != INF && dist[u] + weight < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + weight;
            }
        }
    }

    for (int[] edge: edges) {
        int u = edge[0], v = edge[1], weight = edge[2];

        if (dist[u] != INF && dist[u] + weight < dist[v]) {
            return new int[] {-1};
        }
    }

    return dist;
}

[!tip] Time Complexity O(VE)

List<Activity> activitySelection(List<Activity> activities) {
    activities.sort(Comparator.compareInt(a -> a.finish));

    Activity last = activites.get(0);
    List<Activity> result = new ArrayList<>();
    result.add(last);

    for (int i = 1; i < activities.size(); i++) {

        if (current.start >= last.finish) {

            last = current;

}

public double fractionalKnapsack(List<Obj> list, int capacity) {
        int n = list.size();

        list.sort((a, b) -> Double.compare(
            (double) b.value / b.weight,
            (double) a.value / a.weight
            ));

        double result = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            Obj current = list.get(i);

            if (current.weight < capacity) {
                result += current.value;
                capacity -= current.weight;
            } else {
                result += ((double) current.value / current.weight) * capacity;
                break;
            }
        }

        return result;
    }

public Node huffmanCodes(String S, int f[], int N) {
        PriorityQueue<Node> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.freq - b.freq);

        for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
            pq.offer(new Node(f[i], S.charAt(i)));
        }

        while (pq.size() > 1) {
            Node left = pq.poll();
            Node right = pq.poll();

            Node merged = new Node(left.freq + right.freq, left, right);
            pq.offer(merged);
        }

        return pq.poll();
    }

public int prims(List<List<Pair>> adjList, int V) {
        boolean[] visited = new boolean[V];
        PriorityQueue<Pair> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.weight - b.weight);

        pq.offer(new Pair(0, 0));

        int result = 0;

        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            Pair current = pq.poll();

            int node = current.v;
            int weight = current.weight;

            if (visited[node]) continue;

            visited[node] = true;
            result += weight;

            for (Pair next : adjList.get(node)) {
                if (!visited[next.v]) {
                    pq.offer(next);
                }
            }
        }

        return result;
    }

docs.text:
public int kruskals(int[][] edges, int E, int V) {
        Arrays.sort(edges, (a, b) -> a[2] - b[2]);

        int result = 0;
        int usedEdges = 0;

        DSU dsu = new DSU(V);

        for (int i = 0; i < E && usedEdges < V - 1; i++) {
            int u = edges[i][0];
            int v = edges[i][1];
            int w = edges[i][2];

            if (dsu.parent(u) != dsu.parent(v)) {
                dsu.union(u, v);
                result += w;
                usedEdges++;
            }
        }

        return result;
    }

    public static class DSU {
        int[] parent;
        int[] rank;

        public DSU(int V) {
            parent = new int[V];
            rank = new int[V];

            for (int i = 0; i < V; i++) {
                parent[i] = i;
                rank[i] = 0;
            }
        }

        public int parent(int x) {
            if (parent[x] != x) {
                parent[x] = parent(parent[x]);
            }

            return parent[x];
        }

        public void union(int x, int y) {
            int px = parent(x);
            int py = parent(y);

            if (px == py) return;

            if (rank[px] < rank[py]) {
                parent[px] = py;
            } else if (rank[px] > rank[py]) {
                parent[py] = px;
            } else {
                parent[py] = px;
                rank[px]++;
            }
        }
    }

docs.title: Dijkstra
docs.text:
public int[] dijkstra(int V, int[][] edges, int src) {
        // code here
        List<List<Pair>> adjList = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < V; i++) {
            adjList.add(new ArrayList<>());
        }

        for (int i = 0; i < edges.length; i++) {
            int u = edges[i][0];
            int v = edges[i][1];
            int w = edges[i][2];

            adjList.get(u).add(new Pair(v, w));
            adjList.get(v).add(new Pair(u, w));
        }

        int[] distance = new int[V];
        Arrays.fill(distance, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
        distance[src] = 0;

        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]);

        pq.offer(new int[] {src, 0});

        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            int[] current = pq.poll();

            int node = current[0];
            int currentDistance = current[1];

            if (currentDistance > distance[node]) continue;

            for (Pair edge : adjList.get(node)) {
                int next = edge.v;
                int weight = edge.w;

                if (distance[node] + weight < distance[next]) {
                    distance[next] = distance[node] + weight;
                    pq.offer(new int[] {next, distance[next]});
                }
            }
        }

        return distance;
    }

docs.title: Job Sequencing

public ArrayList<Integer> jobSequencing(int[] deadline, int[] profit) {
        // code here
        int n = deadline.length;

        int[][] jobs = new int[n][2];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            jobs[i][0] = profit[i];
            jobs[i][1] = deadline[i];
        }

        Arrays.sort(jobs, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(b[0], a[0]));

        int maxDeadline = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

        for (int d : deadline) maxDeadline = Math.max(maxDeadline, d);

        int[] slot = new int[maxDeadline];
        Arrays.fill(slot, -1);

        int maxProfit = 0;
        int count = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int d = jobs[i][1] - 1;

            while (d >= 0) {
                if (slot[d] == -1) {
                    slot[d] = i;
                    maxProfit += jobs[i][0];
                    count++;
                    break;
                }
                d--;
            }
        }

        ArrayList<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        result.add(count);
        result.add(maxProfit);

        return result;
    }

docs.title: 3 SAT to Independent Set
docs.text:
• In each clause, there will be only 3 variables
  • draw graphs from the input
    • for each clause, draw a triangle graph
    • from each triangle, connect x to other triangles if x'
      • i.e., if there is x in one triangle, draw a edge to all x' in other triangles
  • After this, find the independent set of size k in this
    • In each triangle, we can choose only one vertex (it is connected to the other 2 in the triangle)
    • Since, we connected all pairs of x and x', it ensures that x and x' will never be true together
    • For the existence of an independent set of size k in the graph, there should be one vertex in each triangle => One true in each clause

docs.title: SAT to 3 SAT
docs.text:
• for clauses of form (l) -> (l or l or l)
  • for clauses of form (l1 or l2) -> (l1 or l2 or l2)
  • for clauses with length, k > 3
    • add extra k - 3 variables: y1, y2, ...y(k-3)
    • (l1 or l2 or l3 or ... or ln)
    • update the clauses as
      • \((l_1 \lor l_2 \lor y_1)\)
      • \((\lnot y_1 \lor l_3 \lor y_2)\)
      • \((\lnot y_2 \lor l_4 \lor y_3)\)
      • ...
      • \((\lnot y_{k-3} \lor l_{k-1} \lor l_k)\)
      • and take the ANDs of them
    • If any of the variable in a clause is true, we will make both the Ys in that clause as false resulting in making all other clauses true
    • If all other variables in a clause is false, we will make the y in the clause as true, making the whole input true only if any of the other clause is true

docs.title: 3 SAT to SAT
docs.text: • 3 SAT is a special case of SAT

docs.title: SAT - Clique
docs.text:
• Construct a graph
    • For each literal in each clause, add a vertex
    • Add edges from vertices of one clause to another such that
      • do not add vertex from x to x'
      • add all other possible edges
  • In this graph, inside one clause, no vertices are connected
  • And between clauses, all pairs other than (x, x') pairs are connected
  • If the CNF is satisfiable, then there will be a clique of size k, because
    • We all edges other than x, x' pair and edges within the clause
    • this means, for a clique of size k to exist, each vertex should be taken from each clause. And since there is no (x, x') pair, these chosen vertices are consistent

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Backend should be configured with an SSL/TLS certificate so that the communication b/w app and backend will be encrypted
  • if backend is ts, we can use class-validator to prevent sql injections
  • rate limit can be set to /send-otp and /login requests

flutter build appbundle --obfuscate --split-debug-info=<path>

docs.title: Payment gateway
docs.text:
• Stripe
  • flutter_stripe

docs.title: Flow of payment
docs.text:
1. User selects a plan in the Flutter app.
  2. The app tells your backend: "This user wants to buy this plan for $10."
  3. Your backend creates a "Payment Intent" with Stripe's API. Stripe returns a client_secret for this transaction.
  4. Your backend sends this client_secret (and only this) back to the Flutter app.
  5. The Flutter app uses the official Stripe SDK and the client_secret to display the native payment sheet (where the user enters card details).
  6. The card details go directly from the user's device to Stripe's servers, bypassing your backend completely.
  7. Stripe processes the payment and notifies the Flutter app of success or failure.
  8. Crucially: The app then notifies your backend that the payment was successful. The backend must verify this by listening to a webhook from Stripe. This prevents a user from tampering with the app to claim a successful payment. Only after your backend receives and verifies the webhook from Stripe should you provision the e-SIM.

docs.title: 1. Introduction to Adversarial Search
docs.text:
Adversarial search is used in "games" where two or more players have conflicting goals. Unlike standard search, the environment is competitive and unpredictable because the opponent’s move is not known in advance.

Types of Games:

  • Deterministic vs. Stochastic: Is there randomness (like dice)?

  • Perfect vs. Imperfect Information: Can you see the whole state (like Chess) or are parts hidden (like Poker)?

docs.title: 2. Formal Definition of a Game
docs.text:
A game is defined by:

  • \(S_0\) (Initial State): The board configuration and whose turn it is.

  • PLAYER(s): Returns which player has the move in state \(s\).

  • ACTIONS(s): Returns the set of legal moves in state \(s\).

  • RESULT(s, a): The transition model (the state resulting from action \(a\) in state \(s\)).

  • TERMINAL-TEST(s): True if the game is over.

  • UTILITY(s, p): The final numeric value for player \(p\) at the end (e.g., \(+1\) for win, \(0\) for tie, \(-1\) for loss).

docs.title: 3. The Minimax Algorithm
docs.text:
Minimax is used to find the optimal strategy for the MAX player, assuming the MIN player also plays optimally.

  • MAX wants to maximize the utility value.

  • MIN wants to minimize the utility value.

The Logic:

For every node, we calculate the Minimax Value:

  1. If it's a leaf node, use its Utility.

  2. If it's a MAX node, take the maximum value of its children.

  3. If it's a MIN node, take the minimum value of its children.

Properties:

  • Completeness: Yes (if the tree is finite).

  • Optimality: Yes (against an optimal opponent).

  • Time Complexity: \(O(b^m)\) (where \(b\) is the branching factor and \(m\) is max depth).

  • Space Complexity: \(O(bm)\) (it performs a depth-first search).

docs.title: 4. Alpha-Beta Pruning
docs.text:
Minimax explores many branches that don't affect the final decision. Alpha-Beta pruning "cuts" these branches to save time.

  • Alpha (\(\alpha\)): The best (highest) value found so far for MAX along the path.

  • Beta (\(\beta\)): The best (lowest) value found so far for MIN along the path.

The Pruning Rule:

If at any point \(\alpha \geq \beta\), we stop searching that branch (prune it).

Complexity Improvements:

  • Worst Case: \(O(b^m)\) (no pruning, occurs if moves are ordered poorly).

  • Best Case (Perfect Ordering): \(O(b^{m/2})\). This means you can search twice as deep in the same amount of time.

docs.title: 5. Real-Time Decisions & Heuristics
docs.text:
In complex games like Chess, the tree is too deep to search to the end (\(b \approx 35, m \approx 100\)). We must stop early.

  1. Cutoff Test: Instead of Terminal-Test, we stop at a certain depth (Depth-limited search).

  2. Heuristic Evaluation Function (\(Eval(s)\)): Estimates the "goodness" of a non-terminal state.

    • Example in Chess: \(Eval(s) = (w_1 \times material\_advantage) + (w_2 \times mobility) + \dots\)

  3. Quiescence Search: To avoid the "horizon effect" (where a move looks good only because the search stopped before the opponent's counter-move), we continue searching "turbulent" states (like captures) until they become "quiet."

docs.title: 6. Games of Chance (Stochastic Games)
docs.text:
In games like Backgammon (with dice), we add Chance Nodes.

  • We use the Expectiminimax algorithm.

  • Value of a Chance Node = \(\sum P(outcome) \times Value(outcome)\).

  • This represents the Expected Value.

docs.title: 7. Imperfect Information Games
docs.text:
In games like Bridge or Poker, you don't know the opponent's hand.

  • Logic: We treat the game as a set of "possible worlds" (all possible card deals consistent with what we see).

  • We calculate the minimax value for each deal and take the average.

docs.title: 1. Variables, Domains, and Constraints for CSP Examples
docs.text:
Using the examples from your files, here is the breakdown into the triplet \((X, D, C)\):

  • Map Coloring :
    • Variables (\(X\)): The regions to be colored (e.g., \(\{WA, NT, Q, NSW, V, SA, T\}\)).
    • Domain (\(D\)): The set of possible colors (e.g., \(\{red, green, blue\}\)).
    • Constraints (\(C\)): Adjacent regions must have different colors (e.g., \(WA \neq NT\), \(WA \neq SA\), etc.).
  • Cryptarithmetic Puzzle (e.g., TWO + TWO = FOUR) :
    • Variables (\(X\)): The unique letters in the puzzle (\(T, W, O, F, U, R\)) and any auxiliary "carry" variables (\(C_1, C_2, C_3\)).
    • Domain (\(D\)): For letters, digits \(\{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\); for carries, typically \(\{0, 1\}\).

    • Constraints (\(C\)):

      • Global constraint: \(AllDiff(T, W, O, F, U, R)\).
      • Arithmetic constraints: e.g., \(O + O = R + 10 \cdot C_1\).
      • Job/Factory Scheduling :
        • Variables (\(X\)): Start and end times for each job or task.
        • Domain (\(D\)): Integers (for discrete days/hours) or Real numbers (for continuous time).
        • Constraints (\(C\)): Precedence rules (e.g., \(StartJob_1 + 5 \leq StartJob_3\)) or resource limitations.

docs.title: 2. Degree Heuristic vs. Least Constraining Value (LCV)
docs.text:
They are not complements; they serve entirely different purposes in the backtracking algorithm:

  • Degree Heuristic (Variable Selection) :
    • What it does: It helps decide which variable to assign next.
    • Logic: It picks the variable that is involved in the most constraints with other unassigned variables.
    • Goal: To fail as early as possible (the "fail-fast" principle) by picking the most difficult variable first.
  • Least Constraining Value (Value Selection) :
    • What it does: Once a variable is picked, it helps decide what order to try its values.
    • Logic: It chooses the value that leaves the maximum number of choices open for neighboring unassigned variables.
    • Goal: To find a solution quickly by picking the value most likely to succeed.

docs.title: 3. Logic Behind Arc Consistency (AC-3)
docs.text:
The logical "idea" behind arc consistency is local restriction enforcement.

The Core Logic: An "arc" from variable \(X\) to \(Y\) is consistent if, for every possible value currently in \(X\)'s domain, there is at least one value in \(Y\)'s domain that satisfies the constraint between them. - Why it works: If \(X\) has a value \(v\) that has no supporting value in \(Y\), then \(v\) can never be part of a valid final solution. By deleting \(v\) now, we prevent the search from ever wasting time trying \(X=v\). - The "Ripple Effect": When we delete a value from \(X\), we must re-check all of \(X\)'s neighbors. If \(X\) now has fewer values, some values in its neighbors might no longer have a "supporting" value in \(X\). This propagation continues until the graph is consistent or a domain becomes empty (indicating failure).

docs.title: 4. Problem Structures and Time Complexity
docs.text: Standard CSPs have a worst-case complexity of \(O(d^n)\). Exploiting structure reduces this: - Independent Subproblems : - Complexity: \(O(\frac{n}{c} \cdot d^c)\) (where \(c\) is the number of variables per component). - Logic: Instead of one large problem, you solve multiple small ones. For \(n=80, c=20, d=2\), the time drops from \(2^{80}\) to roughly \(4 \cdot 2^{20}\), which is nearly linear in \(n\). - Tree-Structured CSPs : - Complexity: \(O(n \cdot d^2)\). - Logic: Since there are no loops, we can use a Topological Sort. We enforce arc consistency from leaves to the root, then assign values from root to leaves. Because each node has only one parent, we only ever have to check \(d\) values of a node against \(d\) values of its parent, leading to \(d^2\) operations per node. - Nearly Tree-Structured (Cutset Conditioning) : - Complexity: \(O(d^c \cdot (n-c)d^2)\) (where \(c\) is the size of the cutset). - Logic: You pick a small set of variables (the cutset) and assign them values in all possible ways (\(d^c\)). For each assignment, the remaining \((n-c)\) variables form a tree, which can be solved in \(O(nd^2)\).

docs.title: 5. Local Search (Iterative Algorithms)
docs.text:
Local search uses a complete-state formulation, meaning it starts with all variables assigned a value, even if they are "illegal" (violate constraints).

How it is done (Min-Conflicts Heuristic):

  1. Start: Assign a value to every variable (usually randomly).

  2. Iterate: Randomly select a variable that currently has a conflict (violates a constraint).

    • Reassign it the value that results in the minimum number of conflicts with all other variables.

  3. End: Stop when no conflicts remain or a max number of steps is reached.

Why it works:

  • It functions like Hill-Climbing where the "height" is the number of violated constraints (\(h(n) = \text{conflicts}\)). By always picking the value that minimizes \(h(n)\), it moves toward a solution.
  • Efficiency: For many problems, like the \(n\)-queens problem, it can find a solution in almost constant time regardless of \(n\) because the "density" of solutions in the search space is high.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
• And what is this AllDiff(...). What does that mean?
  • So, if for some value for x for X, there is no corresponding value y for Y, then are we deleting x from X or just stop testing that branch and starts a new branch of testing?

docs.title: 1. What is the AllDiff(...) Constraint?
docs.text:
The AllDiff constraint is a Global Constraint. It is a compact way to represent a complex rule that applies to many variables simultaneously.

  • Meaning: It specifies that every variable in the list must be assigned a distinct value. No two variables can have the same value.

  • Example (Cryptarithmetic): In the puzzle TWO + TWO = FOUR, the constraint AllDiff(F, T, U, W, R, O) means that each letter must represent a unique digit from 0 to 9.

  • Why use it? Instead of writing many individual binary constraints (e.g., \(F eq T\), \(F eq U\), \(T eq U\), etc.), you use one AllDiff to cover them all. Special-purpose algorithms can handle this constraint much more efficiently than checking all the binary pairs.

docs.title: 2. Arc Consistency: Deleting Values vs. Stopping a Branch
docs.text:
You are touching on the difference between Constraint Propagation and Backtracking Search.

In Arc Consistency (AC-3):

  • You delete the value: If for a value \(x\) in variable \(X\), there is no possible value \(y\) in variable \(Y\) that satisfies the constraint, then \(x\) is deleted from the domain of \(X\).

  • Why? Because if \(x\) has no "support" in \(Y\), it is impossible for \(X=x\) to ever be part of a final, complete solution.

  • Logical Flow:

    1. Pick an arc \(X \rightarrow Y\).

    2. Check every value \(x\) in \(X\)'s domain.

    3. If a value \(x\) is inconsistent with all values in \(Y\), remove \(x\) from the domain of \(X\).

    4. If \(X\)'s domain was changed, add all neighbors of \(X\) back to the queue to be re-checked.

When do you stop the branch?

  • You only "stop testing that branch" if a variable's domain becomes completely empty.
  • An empty domain means that for the current set of assignments, there is no possible value left for that variable. At this point, the algorithm fails and backtracks to the previous variable to try a different value.

Summary: Arc consistency "shrinks" the search space by deleting impossible values. If it shrinks a domain to zero, then the search branch is dead.

docs.title: 1. The Core Logic: Remove-Inconsistent-Values
docs.text:
This is the helper function that checks a single directed arc \((X_i \to X_j)\).

  • Goal: Ensure that for every remaining value \(x\) in \(X_i\), there is at least one "partner" value \(y\) in \(X_j\) that satisfies the constraint between them.

  • Action: If a value \(x\) in \(X_i\) has no support in \(X_j\), it is impossible for \(X_i = x\) to be part of a valid solution. Therefore, we delete \(x\) from the domain of \(X_i\).

  • Return: It returns true if it deleted at least one value, signaling that \(X_i\) has changed.

docs.title: 2. The Main Loop: AC-3
docs.text:
The main algorithm manages a queue of arcs that need to be checked.

  1. Initialization: Every directed arc in the CSP is added to the queue. (Note: If there is a constraint between \(X\) and \(Y\), we add two arcs: \((X, Y)\) and \((Y, X)\)).

  2. Processing: We pull an arc \((X_i, X_j)\) off the queue and run Remove-Inconsistent-Values.

  3. Propagation (The "Why"): If we successfully deleted a value from \(X_i\), we have potentially created a "ripple effect."

    • Because \(X_i\) now has fewer values, its neighbors (\(X_k\)) might now have values that no longer have a partner in \(X_i\).

    • Action: We take all neighbors of \(X_i\) (excluding \(X_j\)) and add those arcs \((X_k, X_i)\) back into the queue to be re-checked.

docs.title: 3. Complexity Analysis: \(O(n^2 d^3)\)
docs.text:
Your notes mention the complexity is \(O(n^2 d^3)\). Here is how that is derived:

  • Variables (\(n\)): Total number of variables.

  • Binary Arcs (\(E\)): In a complete graph, there are \(O(n^2)\) arcs.

  • Domain Size (\(d\)): Maximum number of values per variable.

Step-by-step math:

  1. In the worst case, each time an arc \((X_k, X_i)\) is pulled from the queue, we compare \(d\) values of \(X_k\) against \(d\) values of \(X_i\). This check takes \(O(d^2)\).

  2. How many times can an arc \((X_k, X_i)\) be put back on the queue? A variable has at most \(d\) values. Each time a value is deleted from \(X_i\), its neighbors are added to the queue. Since \(X_i\) can only lose \(d\) values, an arc can be inserted into the queue at most \(d\) times.

  3. Total Complexity = (Number of Arcs \(n^2\)) \(\times\) (Max insertions per arc \(d\)) \(\times\) (Check cost \(d^2\)) = \(O(n^2 d^3)\).

Note: More advanced versions (AC-4) can reach \(O(n^2 d^2)\) by keeping track of specific "supports" for each value, but AC-3 is usually preferred because it has less overhead in practice.

docs.title: 4. Important Exam "Gotcha"
docs.text:
• Arc Consistency is NOT a full solver: It only prunes impossible values. Just because a CSP is "Arc Consistent" does not mean it has a solution. You might have a "consistent" graph where every value has a partner, but you still cannot pick a set of values for all variables simultaneously without a conflict.

  • Detecting all failures: As your text mentions, detecting every possible inconsistency is NP-hard. AC-3 only detects local inconsistencies between pairs of variables.

docs.title: Constraint Satisfaction
docs.text: To prepare for your AI exam, here is a detailed guide on Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs), compiled from your reference materials.

docs.title: 1. What is a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP)?
docs.text:
In standard search, a state is a "black box" (atomic view). In a CSP, the state has a factored view, defined by a set of variables and their values.

A CSP consists of three components:

  • Variables (\(X\)): A set of variables \(\{X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\}\).
  • Domains (\(D\)): A set of possible values for each variable \(\{D_1, D_2, \dots, D_n\}\).
  • Constraints (\(C\)): Rules that specify allowable combinations of values for subsets of variables.

Example: Map Coloring

  • Variables: States like WA, NT, Q, NSW, V, SA, T.
  • Domain: \(\{Red, Green, Blue\}\).
  • Constraints: Adjacent regions must have different colors (e.g., \(WA \neq NT\)).

docs.title: Varieties of CSPs
docs.text:
• Discrete Variables:

    • Finite Domains: e.g., Map coloring or Boolean SAT.
    • Infinite Domains: e.g., Job scheduling where variables are start/end days. These require a constraint language (e.g., \(StartJob_1 + 5 \leq StartJob_3\)).
    • Continuous Variables: e.g., Scheduling the Hubble Telescope. These can often be solved in polynomial time using Linear Programming.

docs.title: Varieties of Constraints
docs.text:
• Unary: Involves a single variable (e.g., \(SA \neq green\)).
  • Binary: Involves pairs of variables (e.g., \(SA \neq WA\)).
  • Higher-order/Global: Involves 3 or more variables, like the Alldiff constraint in Cryptarithmetic puzzles.
  • Soft Constraints (Preferences): Represented by costs for assignments, leading to Constraint Optimization Problems.

docs.title: 3. Backtracking Search
docs.text: The basic uninformed algorithm for solving CSPs is Backtracking Search, which is a depth-first search that chooses values for one variable at a time and "backtracks" when a variable has no legal values left.

docs.title: Heuristics to Improve Backtracking:
docs.text:
To make backtracking efficient, we use three main heuristics:

  1. Minimum Remaining Values (MRV): Choose the variable with the fewest "legal" values left. This is also called the "most constrained variable" heuristic.
  2. Degree Heuristic: Choose the variable that participates in the largest number of constraints on other unassigned variables (used as a tie-breaker for MRV).
  3. Least Constraining Value: Given a variable, choose the value that rules out the fewest choices for the neighboring variables.

docs.title: 4. Constraint Propagation (Early Failure Detection)
docs.text:
Instead of waiting for a "dead end," we can detect failures early:

  • Forward Checking: Whenever a variable \(X\) is assigned, the algorithm looks at each unassigned variable \(Y\) connected to \(X\) and deletes any value from \(Y\)'s domain that inconsistent with \(X\)'s assignment.
  • Arc Consistency (AC-3): A more powerful method. An arc \(X \rightarrow Y\) is "consistent" if for every value in \(X\), there is some allowed value in \(Y\). If \(X\) loses a value, its neighbors must be re-checked.

docs.title: 5. Problem Structure
docs.text:
• Independent Subproblems: If the constraint graph has connected components that aren't linked, they can be solved separately (e.g., Tasmania in the map coloring example).
  • Tree-Structured CSPs: If the graph has no loops, it can be solved in \(O(nd^2)\) time, which is linear in the number of variables.
  • Nearly Tree-Structured (Cutset Conditioning): You can remove a small set of variables (a cutset) to turn the remaining graph into a tree.

docs.title: 6. Local Search (Iterative Algorithms)
docs.text:
Local search uses "complete-state" formulation, meaning all variables are assigned a value from the start, even if they violate constraints.

  • Min-Conflicts Heuristic: Randomly select a conflicted variable and change its value to the one that results in the minimum number of conflicts with other variables.

  • Performance: Surprisingly, min-conflicts can solve problems like the n-queens problem for \(n = 10,000,000\) in almost constant time.

docs.title: Step 1: Preprocessing (Topological Sort)
docs.text:
First, you pick any arbitrary variable to be the Root. You then order the variables such that each node appears in the list after its parent.

  • Example: In the graph \(A \to B, A \to C\), the ordering would be \((A, B, C)\). \(A\) is the parent of \(B\) and \(C\).

  • The Goal: This creates a clear "hierarchy" so we know the direction in which constraints should be enforced.

docs.title: Step 2: Backward Pass (Ensuring Consistency)
docs.text:
"For \(j\) from \(n\) down to \(2\), apply RemoveInconsistent(Parent(Xj), Xj)"

In this phase, we move from the leaves up to the root.

  • The Logic: We look at every node \(X_j\) and its parent. We remove any values from the parent's domain that don't have a matching valid value in \(X_j\).

  • Why it works: By the time we reach the root, we have guaranteed that for every value remaining in the root, there is at least one "path" of valid assignments all the way down to the leaves.

  • Crucial Point: This step ensures that we will never have to backtrack. If the root's domain isn't empty after this, a solution is guaranteed to exist.

docs.title: Step 3: Forward Pass (Assignment)
docs.text:
"For \(j\) from \(1\) to \(n\), assign \(X_j\) consistently with \(Parent(X_j)\)"

Now we move from the root down to the leaves.

  1. Pick any remaining legal value for the root \(X_1\).

  2. For the next variable \(X_2\) (a child of the root), pick a value that is consistent with the value already assigned to \(X_1\).

  3. Because of the "Backward Pass" we did in Step 2, we are mathematically certain that such a value exists.

docs.title: Why is the complexity \(O(nd^2)\)?
docs.text:
1. Topological Sort: Takes \(O(n)\) time.

  2. Backward Pass: There are \(n-1\) arcs in a tree. For each arc, we compare \(d\) values of the parent against \(d\) values of the child. That is \((n-1) \times d^2\).

  3. Forward Pass: For each node, we just pick one value that works with its parent. This takes \(O(nd)\).

  4. Total: \(O(nd^2)\).

docs.title: Summary for Exam:
docs.text: The beauty of this algorithm is that Arc Consistency is sufficient for trees. In a general graph, arc consistency doesn't guarantee a solution (you still need to search). But in a tree, once you have enforced arc consistency from the leaves up, you can assign values greedily from the top down without ever hitting a dead end.

docs.title: A star Search
docs.text:
\[f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\]

g(n) = cost from start to n h(n) = estimated cost from n to goal f(n) = estimated total path cost through n

docs.title: Admissible Heuristics
docs.text: $\(h(n) \le h^*(n) \space \forall \space n\)$ - Means, we should not overestimate true cost - We should be optimistic

docs.title: Consistent Heuristics
docs.text:
$\(h(n) \le h(n') + c(n, a, n')\)$ - Means, estimate at parent ≤ step cost + estimate at child

Every consistent heuristic is admissible

Property Value Complete ✅ Yes Time \(O(b^d)\) Space \(O(b^d)\) Optimal ✅ Yes (if admissible/consistent) # Optimality of A* - proof - Let G be the optimal solution - And \(G_2\) be a sub-optimal solution

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{Since } G_2 \text{ is a solution, } \ h(G_2) &= 0 \ \implies f(G_2) &= g(G_2) \ \text {Similarly since G is a solution, } \ h(G) &= 0 \ \implies f(G) &= 0 \ \text {Since G is the optimal solution and } G_2 \text{ is suboptimal} \ g(G) &< g(G_2) \ \forall n, f(n) &\le f(G) \ \implies f(G_2) &\gt f(G) \ \end{aligned} $$ - therefore we don't expand the path to \(G_2\) instead of G

docs.text:

    • Choose node with smallest h(n)

    • Repeat

docs.text: • Instead of blindly searching, we now choose the successor based on some heuristics

docs.text:

  • It measures the goodness of the node
  • Its designed mostly using intuition
  • example (City Map)

    • Heuristic = Straight line distance between current node and goal node

  • This ensures the space complexity stays in \(O(bd)\) instead of exponential

docs.text:

  • typically w = 5

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
$$ \begin{aligned} y &= w_0 + w_1x \ \bar x &= \frac{1}{N}\sum (x) \ \bar y &= \frac{1}{N}\sum (y) \ w_1 &= \frac{\sum ((x_i - \bar x) \times (y_i - \bar y))}{\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2} \ w_0 &= \bar y - w_1 \bar x \\

\end{aligned} $$

docs.title: 🔷 1. From scalar to vector (why we even need this)
docs.text:
In simple (univariate) regression:

\[f(x) = w_0 + w_1 x\]

But in real life, you have multiple features:

  • (x_1): budget

  • (x_2): actors

  • (x_3): marketing

  • ...

So the model becomes:

\[f(x) = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_D x_D \]

This is messy to write repeatedly. So we convert everything into vectors

docs.title: 🔷 2. Vector representation of a single data point
docs.text:
We rewrite the input as a vector:

\[x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_D \\ \end{bmatrix} \]

👉 The 1 is added for bias ((w_0))

Weights also become a vector:

\[w = \begin{bmatrix} w_0 \\ w_1 \\ w_2 \\ \vdots \\ w_D \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: 🔷 3. Prediction becomes a dot product
docs.text:
Now the model simplifies beautifully:

$$f(x) = w^T x $$ $$f(x)=w^T x $$ 👉 This is just a dot product: $$w^T x = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + \dots + w_D x_D $$ So instead of a long equation, it's just one operation.

docs.title: 🔷 4. From one data point → all data (Matrix form)
docs.text:
Now suppose you have N data points.

We stack all inputs into a matrix:

\[X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1D} \\ 1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{2D} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{N1} & x_{N2} & \dots & x_{ND} \\ \end{bmatrix} \]

👉 This is called the design matrix

Targets:

\[y = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_N \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: 🔷 5. Entire prediction in one line
docs.text:
Now predictions for all data:

$\(\hat{y} = X w\)$ 👉 This is powerful:

  • No loops

  • Fully vectorized

  • Efficient in computation

docs.title: 🔷 6. Error (loss) in matrix form
docs.text:
Original loss (scalar form):

\[J(w) = \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (f(x_i) - y_i)^2\]

Matrix form:

\[J(w) = \frac{1}{2} |Xw - y|^2\] \[J(w)=\frac{1}{2}||Xw-y||^2\]

👉 Interpretation:

  • (Xw) → predictions

  • (y) → actual values

  • Difference → error vector

  • Norm → total squared error

docs.title: 🔷 7. Expanding the loss (important for derivation)
docs.text:
\[J(w) = \frac{1}{2}(Xw - y)^T (Xw - y)\]

Expanding:

\[= \frac{1}{2}(w^T X^T X w - 2 w^T X^T y + y^T y)\]

👉 This form is useful for:

  • taking derivatives

  • finding closed-form solution

docs.title: 🔷 8. Gradient (key insight)
docs.text:
Using vector calculus:

[ \nabla_w J(w) = X^T (Xw - y) ]

\nabla_w J(w)=X^T(Xw-y)

👉 Interpretation:

  • (Xw - y): error

  • (X^T): distributes error back to weights

docs.title: 🔷 9. Closed-form solution (Normal Equation)
docs.text:
Set gradient = 0:

[ X^T X w = X^T y ]

Solution:

[ w = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y ]

w=(X^T X)^{-1}X^T y

👉 This gives optimal weights directly (no iteration needed)

docs.title: Think geometrically:
docs.text:
• Each column of (X) = a feature direction

  • (Xw) = combination of those directions

  • We are trying to project (y) onto the column space of (X)

👉 Linear regression = best projection problem

docs.title: 🔷 11. Why this matrix form is powerful
✅ Clean
docs.text: One equation replaces many sums

docs.title: ✅ Fast
docs.text: Uses optimized linear algebra libraries

docs.title: ✅ Scalable
docs.text:
Works for:

  • millions of samples

  • thousands of features

docs.title: ✅ Extensible
docs.text:
Same form works for:

  • regularization

  • neural networks

  • kernel methods

docs.title: 🔷 12. Big Picture Summary
docs.text:
Concept Scalar Form Matrix Form Model (w_0 + w_1 x_1 + ...) (w^T x) Dataset loop over samples (X) matrix Prediction loop (Xw) Loss sum of squares (|Xw - y|^2) Solution iterative ((X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty)

If you want, next we can go even deeper into:

  • geometric intuition (projection, orthogonality)

  • why (X^TX) must be invertible

  • connection to gradient descent vs closed-form

Just tell me 👍

DFS BFS Space efficient Space heavy Not optimal Optimal (equal cost) Can go very deep Explores evenly

docs.text:

    • Forward search (start to goal)
    • Backward search (goal to start)
  • Stop when they meet

docs.title: DFS
docs.text:
• Open list is a Stack in DFS

Time complexity = \(O(b^d)\) Space complexity = \(O(bd)\) Completeness = true for finite state space Optimal = false

docs.text: • Very space efficient

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• May find a very deep bad solution
  • Not optimal
  • Can get stuck in deep branches

docs.title: Iterative Deepening Search
docs.text:
• Run DFS with depth limit incrementing at each iteration
  • i.e., nodes explored in each iteration is
    • \(1 + b + b^2 + b^3 + ... + b^d\)
    • \(O(b^d)\)

Time Complexity = \(O(b^d)\) Space Complexity = \(O(bd)\) like DFS Completeness = true Optimal = true if costs are equal

  • Is optimal because, if the cost is same, then solutions in a single level are all optimal solutions.
  • Since we are incrementing the depth limit each time, we will ensure that the first solution which is the optimal one will be found.

docs.title: Uniform Cost Search
docs.text:
• Open list is a Priority Queue/Min Heap in UCS
  • Just like dijkstra, but stop the algorithm when we reach the goal state

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Iterative lengthening
    • Like iterative deepening, but limit on cost instead of depth

docs.title: Uninformed Search
docs.text:
• We search the search space blindly.
    • No heuristics
    • No estimated distance to goal
    • No domain knowledge

  • Only know

    • initial state
    • next possible states from current state
    • to check whether current state is the goal state

  • We need to check

    • completeness
    • time complexity
    • space complexity
    • optimality

docs.text:
• Open list = states to explore
  • Closed list = states which are already explored

b = branching factor d = depth of goal m = maximum depth of the tree \(C^*\) = optimal solution cost \(\epsilon\) = minimum step cost
