docs.title: THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE PRIMARY MARKET AND SECONDARY MARKET
docs.text:
1. The Primary Market refers to the market in which new securities are issued by the company to the public for the first time while the secondary market refers to the market where new securities which are already issued are traded.
  2. There is a direct involvement of the company in the primary market. Whereas, in the secondary market, the company has virtually no involvement since the transactions take place between the investors.
  3. The primary market deals with new securities, that is, securities, which were not previously available and are, therefore, offered to the investing public for the first time while the secondary market is market for already issued securities.
  4. The primary market provides additional funds to the issuing companies either by starting a new enterprise or for the expansion or diversification of the existing business. On the other hand, the secondary market does not provide additional funds since the company is not involved in the transaction.

docs.title: PARTICIPANTS IN THE CAPITAL MARKET
docs.text:
1. INVESTORS: Investors are the lifeline of any capital market. For a vibrant capital market, the capital market should be able to attract the savings of investors. Investors belong to various categories such as Retail Investors, Institutional Investors like mutual funds, insurance companies and Foreign Portfolio Investors.
  2. STOCK EXCHANGE: Stock exchange is a place, where securities issued by issuer companies are listed and traded. The term is synonymously used for secondary markets.
  3. DEPOSITORY: A depository is an organisation which holds securities (like shares, debentures, bonds, government securities, mutual fund units etc.) of investors in electronic form at the request of the investors through a registered Depository Participant. They also provide safekeeping of securities. They also help in other functions like pledge, hypothecation, stock lending and borrowing etc. In India, there are two depositories namely National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) and Central Depository Services (India) Limited (CDSL).
  4. INTERMEDIARIES: Intermediaries are those entities which offer various services in relation to the capital markets. There are various categories of intermediaries such as stockbrokers, merchant bankers, underwriters etc.

docs.title: CAPITAL MARKET INSTRUMENTS

docs.title: FEATURES OF SHARES
docs.text:
1. Profits of companies are sometimes paid in the form of dividends. A higher proportion of shares in a company signifies a higher stake in the profits also. In case of bankruptcy and liquidation, shareholders receive what is left after all the creditors have been paid.
  2. Another extremely important feature of a share is its limited liability, which means that, as an owner of a share, you are not personally liable if the company is not able to pay its debts.
  3. Companies issue shares to raise capital as it does not require them to pay back the money after a certain period (other than redeemable preference shares) or make interest payments continuously. Equity shares can be held by the company till perpetuity.
  4. The investors in equity shares make money either through dividends or through capital appreciation in the price of the shares. Equity shares are very high-risk instruments with no guaranteed returns. There is always a risk of downside in the value of equity investments.
  5. Shares are traded at market value on stock exchanges. Market value per share is the current price at which the share is traded.

docs.title: FEATURES OF EQUITY SHARES

docs.title: ADR VS GDR:
docs.text:
1. ADR and GDR are commonly used by the Indian companies to raise funds from the foreign capital market.
  2. The principal difference between ADR and GDR is in the market in which they are issued and the exchange in which they are listed.
  3. While ADR is traded on U.S. Stock Exchanges, GDR is traded on European Stock Exchanges.
  4. While ADR is issued by a U.S. bank, GDR is issued by the international depository bank, representing foreign company’s stock trading globally.
  5. Through ADR issue, funds can be raised in US stock market.; Through GDR issue, funds can be raised in any country’s stock market except USA.

docs.title: FUNCTIONS OF SEBI
docs.text:
1. regulate the business in stock exchanges and any other securities market.
  2. register and regulate the working of stock brokers, sub-brokers, share transfer agents, bankers to an issue, trustees of trust deeds, registrars to an issue, merchant bankers, underwriters, portfolio managers, investment advisers and such other intermediaries who may be associated with securities market in any manner;
  3. register and regulate the working of the depositories, participants, custodians of securities, foreign institutional investors, credit rating agencies and such other intermediaries as the Board may, by notification, specify in this behalf;
  4. register and regulate the working of venture capital funds and collective investment schemes, including mutual funds;
  5. promote and regulate self-regulatory organisations;
  6. prohibit fraudulent and unfair trade practices relating to securities market;
  7. promote investors’ education and train the intermediaries of securities markets;
  8. prohibit insider trading in securities;
  9. regulate substantial acquisition of shares and takeover of companies;
  10. call for information from, undertaking inspection, conducting inquiries and audits of the stock exchanges, mutual funds, other persons associated with the securities market, intermediaries and self-regulatory organisations in the securities market;
  11. call for information and records from any person including any bank or any other authority or board or corporation established or constituted by or under any Central or State Act which, in the opinion of the Board, shall be relevant to any investigation or inquiry by the Board in respect of any transaction in securities.

docs.title: POWERS OF SEBI
docs.text:
1. suspend the trading of any security in a recognised stock exchange;
  2. restrain persons from accessing the securities market and prohibit any person associated with securities market to buy, sell or deal in securities;
  3. suspend any office-bearer of any stock exchange or self-regulatory organisation from holding such position;
  4. impound and retain the proceeds or securities in respect of any transaction which is under investigation.
  5. prohibit any company from issuing prospectus, any offer document, or advertisement soliciting money from the public for the issue of securities;
  6. specify the conditions subject to which the prospectus, such offer document or advertisement, if not prohibited may be issued;
  7. specify the requirements for listing and transfer of securities.
  8. the transactions in securities are being dealt with in a manner detrimental to the investors or the securities market; or
  9. any intermediary or any person associated with the securities market has violated any of the provisions of the SEBI Act or the rules or the regulations made or directions issued by the Board.

docs.title: Indian Financial System
docs.text: These detailed notes cover the entire structure of the Indian Financial System as presented in the source "3_INDIAN FINANCIAL SYSTEM.pdf".

docs.title: I. Overview of the Indian Financial System
docs.text:
• Definition: A network consisting of financial institutions, markets, instruments, and services that facilitate the transmission of money between households (savers) and entities (investors).
  • Integral Components: Banks, stock exchanges, insurance companies, and various financial institutions.

docs.title: 1. Department of Economic Affairs (DEA)
docs.text:
• Located under the Ministry of Finance, it is the nodal agency for formulating and monitoring economic policies and managing the Union Budget.
  • Oversees public finance, debt, and foreign exchange.
  • Regulates capital markets, including stock exchanges and commodity derivatives.
  • Manages administrative matters for SEBI and the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT).

docs.title: 2. Ministry of Corporate Affairs (formerly DCA)
docs.text:
• Administers laws like the Companies Act to ensure corporate transparency and accountability.
  • Promotes good governance, investigates fraud, and supervises professional bodies like ICAI and ICSI to build investor confidence.

docs.title: 3. Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
docs.text:
• A statutory body established on April 12, 1992, to regulate the Indian securities market.
  • Targets three categories:
    • Issuers: Provides a marketplace to raise finance.
    • Investors: Ensures safety and provides accurate information.
    • Intermediaries: Enables a competitive professional market.
  • Regulates venture capital funds, mutual funds, and collective investment schemes.
  • Prohibits fraudulent and unfair trade practices.

docs.title: 4. Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
docs.text:
• Established April 1, 1935; the central bank and apex authority for all banks.
  • Core Functions:
    • Monetary Authority: Implements and monitors monetary policy.
    • Supervisor: Prescribes parameters for banking operations.
    • Foreign Exchange Manager: Manages reserves and the external value of the Rupee under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999.
    • Currency Issuer: Issues, exchanges, and destroys currency notes.
    • Payment Systems Supervisor: Upgrades systems like UPI, NEFT, and RTGS.
    • Banker to Government: Acts as a financial advisor and merchant banker, managing public debt and government securities (T-bills and bonds).

docs.title: 5. Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA)
docs.text:
• Established in 1999 to promote, regulate, and ensure the growth of the insurance sector.
  • Grants licenses to insurers and protects the interests of policyholders through ethical standards and grievance redressal.

docs.title: III. Financial Institutions and Intermediaries
docs.text: Organizations that act as a bridge between investors (surplus funds) and borrowers (need for funds) by redistributing money through loans and mortgages.

docs.title: 1. Scheduled Banks
docs.text:
Banks covered under the 2nd Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934. They are eligible for RBI loans at the bank rate and membership in clearing houses.

  • Commercial Banks: Profit-making institutions that accept deposits (borrowing rate) and lend loans (lending rate).
    • Public Sector Banks (PSBs): Majority held by the Government (e.g., SBI, PNB).
    • Private Sector Banks: Owned by private individuals (e.g., ICICI, HDFC).
    • Foreign Banks: Owned by foreign entities (e.g., HSBC, Citi Bank).
    • Regional Rural Banks (RRBs): Owned by Central Govt, State Govt, and Sponsor Banks in a 50:15:35 ratio.
  • Cooperative Banks: Owned and operated by cooperative societies on a non-profit (no profit, no loss) basis. They are registered under State Cooperative Acts and classified into Urban (UCBs) and Rural (RCBs).

docs.title: 2. Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)
docs.text:
Companies registered under the Companies Act engaged in loans, securities acquisition, leasing, hire-purchase, and insurance.

  • Key Distinctions from Banks:
    • Cannot accept demand deposits (repayable on demand).
    • Cannot issue cheques or form part of the payment/settlement system.
    • Not required to maintain the same reserve ratios or lending restrictions as banks.
    • Income is primarily fee-based (premiums, management fees) rather than interest-spread.

docs.title: IV. Specialized Financial Entities
docs.text:
• Stock Exchanges: Markets (like NSE and BSE) where listed companies trade stocks, bonds, and commodities.
  • Insurance Companies: NBFCs regulated by IRDA.
    • Life Insurance: Covers life uncertainties; includes Whole Life (payout to nominee on death) and Joint Life (group cover) policies.
    • General Insurance: Includes Fire, Marine (Cargo, Freight, Hull), and Miscellaneous insurance.
  • Mutual Funds: Investment vehicles that pool money into diversified portfolios of securities. Managed by Asset Management Companies (AMCs).
  • Unit Trust of India (UTI): Established in 1964 to encourage small savings; now UTI Mutual Fund.
  • Investment & Merchant Bankers:
    • Investment Banks: Advise on M&A and help companies raise money by selling securities.
    • Merchant Bankers: Specialized firms providing capital raising, corporate advisory, and portfolio management for corporations and wealthy individuals.
  • Pension Funds: Invest money to provide retirement income for workers.
  • Private Equity & Venture Capital: Invest in private companies or early-stage startups with high growth potential.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: These notes provide a comprehensive overview of the material contained in the source document "1C_BUSINESS_INTRODUCTION.pdf".

docs.title: I. Introduction to Business
docs.text:
• Purpose of Business: While making money is a primary goal, business is about much more than profit; it contributes significantly to the growth and development of a country.
  • The Business Cycle: Business activities are central to life, starting with production and ending with consumption. People satisfy their needs by purchasing goods and services from various markets, whether physical or electronic.
  • Supply Chain: Different groups of people engage in economic activities like production, manufacturing, and distribution to make these products available.

docs.title: II. Historical Context of Business in India
docs.text:
• Ancient Prosperity: Trading in ancient India generated surplus income through internal and foreign trade. Between the 1st and 7th centuries, India was the largest economy in the world, controlling roughly one-fourth to one-third of the world’s wealth.
  • Indigenous Banking: A dominant indigenous banking system evolved to finance trade, agriculture, and manufacturing, facilitating credit transactions and loans.
  • Trade Centres and Goods: Major trade centres included Peshawar, Taxila, Indraprastha, Surat, and Ujjain.
    • Exports: Spices, wheat, sugar, cotton, and live animals.
    • Imports: Horses, Chinese silks, linen, gold, silver, and wine.
  • Economic Shifts: Under British rule, India shifted from being an exporter of processed goods to an exporter of raw materials and a buyer of manufactured goods.
  • Post-Independence and 1991 Reforms: After 1947, India focused on centralized planning and public investment. Severe balance of payment issues led to the 1991 Economic Liberalization, adopting the LPG approach (Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalisation).
  • Recent Initiatives: Current government programs like "Make in India," "Skill India," and "Digital India" are expected to further boost the economy.

docs.title: III. The Concept and Characteristics of Business
docs.text:
• Definition: Derived from the word "busy," business refers to an occupation where people regularly engage in the purchase, production, or sale of goods and services to earn profit.
  • Economic vs. Non-Economic: Activities are classified as economic (undertaken to earn a livelihood) or non-economic (undertaken out of love, sympathy, or emotion). Business is strictly an economic activity.

docs.title: Core Characteristics of Business Activities:
docs.text:
1. Economic Activity: Motivated by earning money rather than emotional factors.
  2. Production or Procurement: Goods (consumable or capital) and services must be produced or acquired before they are offered to users.
  3. Sale or Exchange: There must be a transfer of goods/services for value; personal consumption does not constitute business.
  4. Regularity: Business involves dealings on a regular basis; a single transaction is not a business activity.
  5. Profit Earning: No business can survive long without profit, which leads businessmen to maximize sales and reduce costs.
  6. Uncertainty of Return: There is no guarantee of the amount of profit that will be earned in a given period.
  7. Element of Risk: Risks arise from unfavorable events like changes in fashion, competition, fire, or natural calamities.

docs.title: IV. Classification of Business Activities
docs.text: Business activities are broadly categorized into Industry and Commerce.

docs.title: 1. Industry
docs.text:
Industry is concerned with converting resources into useful goods, often involving mechanical appliances and technical skills.

  • Primary Industries: Concerned with the extraction of natural resources and reproduction of living organisms.
    • Extractive: Farming, mining, fishing, and hunting.
    • Genetic: Breeding plants (nurseries) and animals (poultry, fish hatcheries).
  • Secondary Industries: Process materials already extracted by the primary sector.
    • Manufacturing: Creating "form utility" by processing raw materials into finished products. This includes Analytical (oil refining), Synthetical (cement), Processing (sugar), and Assembling (cars/computers).
    • Construction: Building dams, bridges, and roads.
  • Tertiary Industries: Provide support services to primary and secondary industries (e.g., transport, banking, insurance).

docs.title: 2. Commerce
docs.text:
Commerce facilitates the exchange of goods and services and links producers with consumers. It is divided into:

  • Trade: The actual buying and selling of goods (internal or external).
  • Auxiliaries to Trade: Activities that assist trade by removing various "hindrances".

docs.title: V. Auxiliaries to Trade (Support Services)
docs.text:
These services remove obstacles that arise during the production and distribution of goods.

  • Transport and Communication: Removes the hindrance of place by moving raw materials to factories and finished goods to consumers.
  • Banking and Finance: Removes the hindrance of finance by providing necessary funds, loans, overdrafts, and credit facilities to businesses.
  • Insurance: Removes the hindrance of risk by providing protection against loss or damage due to fire, theft, or accidents in exchange for a premium.
  • Warehousing: Removes the hindrance of time by providing storage for goods that are not consumed immediately, helping maintain reasonable price levels.
  • Advertising and Public Relations: Removes the hindrance of information.
    • Advertising: A paid activity used to inform and persuade customers about product features and prices.
    • Public Relations (PR): Often unpaid, strategic communication used to build mutually beneficial relationships (e.g., press releases).

docs.title: Money Market
docs.text: These comprehensive notes cover the structure, participants, and instruments of the Indian Money Market as detailed in the source "5D. MONEY MARKET (1).pdf", with additional context from the "INDIAN FINANCIAL SYSTEM" and "RESERVE BANK OF INDIA" sources.

docs.title: I. Concept and Objectives of the Money Market
docs.text:
• Definition: The money market deals with short-term securities with a maturity of less than one year. Because these assets are close substitutes for cash, they are often called "near money instruments".
  • Core Objectives:
    • To provide short-term funds to borrowers at reasonable interest rates.
    • To provide a platform for individuals and companies to park surplus funds and earn returns.
    • To assist the RBI in implementing monetary policies through Open Market Operations (OMO).
    • To help the Government raise funds to meet its fiscal deficit.

docs.title: II. Key Characteristics and Functions
docs.text:
1. Short-term Maturity: Trading is limited to instruments with a maturity of under one year, allowing investors to adjust strategies quickly.
  2. Low Risk: Instruments are issued by highly creditworthy entities (Governments, large corporations), significantly reducing default risk.
  3. High Liquidity: Investors can buy or sell these instruments quickly with minimal transaction costs.
  4. Fixed Income: Investments offer a predetermined interest rate, ensuring a regular and predictable cash flow.
  5. Diversification: Investors can spread risk across various industries, issuers, and maturities (e.g., T-bills, CPs, CDs).
  6. Regulated Market: The market is strictly monitored by the RBI, which boosts investor confidence.
  7. Benchmark Rates: Money market rates influence other borrowing and lending rates throughout the economy, such as interbank lending rates.

docs.title: III. Participants in the Money Market
docs.text:
• RBI: Implements monetary policy and maintains stability by buying/selling instruments to control money supply.
  • Government: Issues short-term securities to fund operations.
  • Commercial Banks: Borrow and lend in the interbank market and invest surplus funds.
  • Financial Institutions: Includes NBFCs, insurance companies, mutual funds, and pension funds seeking short-term returns.
  • Primary Dealers: Authorized by the RBI to act as intermediaries in government securities auctions.
  • Individuals: Participate by investing their surplus cash in available instruments.

docs.title: IV. Money Market vs. Capital Market
docs.text: Feature Money Market Capital Market Maturity Short-term (1 year or less) Long-term (More than 1 year) Instruments T-bills, CP, CD, Repos Stocks, bonds, debentures Risk/Liquidity Less risky and highly liquid More risky and less liquid Regulator RBI SEBI Purpose Working capital/short-term needs Fixed capital/long-term growth

docs.title: V. Market Segments
docs.text:
1. Unorganised Money Market: Informal, unregulated, and high-risk lending with limited documentation. Participants include Indigenous Bankers, Money Lenders, and unregulated NBFIs like chit funds.
  2. Organised Money Market: Formal and structured sector supervised by regulatory bodies.

docs.title: VI. Detailed Instruments of the Organised Money Market
1. Call and Notice Money
docs.text:
• Used by banks for interbank transactions to meet Cash Reserve Requirements (CRR).
  • Call Money: Lent for one day (overnight).
  • Notice Money: Lent for 2 to 14 days.
  • It is highly liquid; the lender can demand funds back at any time. Interest rates are called "call rates".

docs.title: 2. Treasury Bills (T-bills)
docs.text:
• Issuer: RBI on behalf of the Central Government to fund short-term needs.
  • Nature: "Zero Coupon Bonds"; they pay no interest but are sold at a discount and redeemed at face value.
  • Maturities: 91-day (weekly), 182-day (fortnightly), and 364-day (monthly).
  • Min. Investment: Rs. 25,000 and multiples thereof.
  • Platform: Issued via the E-Kuber electronic platform.

docs.title: 3. Certificate of Deposit (CD)
docs.text:
• A negotiable, unsecured instrument issued by scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs) and select All-India Financial Institutions.
  • Min. Amount: Rs. 1 lakh and multiples thereof.
  • Tenure: 7 days to 1 year for banks; 1 to 3 years for Financial Institutions.
  • Must have a minimum investment-grade credit rating to be issued.

docs.title: 4. Commercial Paper (CP)
docs.text:
• An unsecured promissory note issued by well-rated, large companies to meet short-term funding needs.
  • Eligibility: Tangible net worth of at least Rs. 4 crore, a minimum A3 credit rating, and a working capital limit of at least Rs. 10 crore.
  • Tenure: 7 days to 1 year.
  • Min. Amount: Rs. 5 lakh and multiples thereof.

docs.title: 5. Commercial Bill
docs.text:
• A negotiable instrument arising from trade transactions (Bill of Exchange).
  • When a bank accepts a trade bill, it becomes a commercial bill.
  • Discounting: The seller can sell the bill to a bank at a discount to get immediate cash before the bill matures (usually 3 months).

docs.title: 6. Repurchase Agreements (Repo & Reverse Repo)
docs.text:
• Repo: Borrowing funds by selling securities with an agreement to repurchase them at a future date and a higher price.
  • Reverse Repo: Lending funds by purchasing securities with an agreement to resell them later.
  • These act as collateralized borrowing typically using Government securities or high-rated (AA or above) corporate debt.

docs.title: 7. Money Market Mutual Funds (MMMF)
docs.text:
• Mutual funds that invest exclusively in money market instruments to allow small investors to participate.
  • They have a minimum lock-in period of 15 days.
  • Since March 2000, they have been regulated by SEBI, while banks still require RBI clearance to set them up.

docs.title: Ownership of Business
docs.text: These notes provide a comprehensive and detailed overview of the ownership and forms of business organizations as presented in "2B_OWNERSHIP OF BUSINESS.pdf".

docs.title: I. Introduction to Business Ownership
docs.text:
There are five primary forms of business organizations. These are categorized into non-professional and professional organizations:

  • Non-Professional: Sole Proprietorship, Partnership, and Joint Hindu Family Business.
  • Professional: Joint Stock Company and Cooperative Societies.

docs.title: II. Sole Proprietorship
docs.text: A business owned, managed, and controlled by a single individual who bears all risks and receives all profits. It is the simplest form of organization and is most suitable for small businesses and personalized services like beauty parlors or retail shops.

docs.title: 1. Key Features
docs.text:
• Formation and Closure: Easy to start and close with minimal legal formalities; no separate law governs it.
  • Unlimited Liability: The owner is personally responsible for debts; personal assets (e.g., a car) can be sold to repay business liabilities.
  • Sole Risk Bearer: The owner alone bears the risk of failure but also enjoys 100% of the profits.
  • Control: Absolute decision-making power rests with the owner without interference.
  • No Separate Entity: Law makes no distinction between the owner and the business.
  • Lack of Continuity: Death, insanity, or bankruptcy of the owner can lead to business closure.

docs.title: 2. Merits and Limitations
docs.text:
• Merits: Prompt decision-making, confidentiality of information, direct incentive to work hard, and a sense of personal accomplishment.
  • Limitations: Resources are limited to personal savings/borrowings, limited life span, and the owner may lack expertise in all managerial areas (purchasing, selling, financing).

docs.title: III. Partnership
docs.text: An association of two or more persons (minimum 2, maximum 50) who agree to carry on a business and share profits/losses. It is governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

docs.title: 1. Key Features
docs.text:
• Formation: Based on a legal agreement (Partnership Deed) for a lawful business with a profit motive.
  • Liability: Partners have unlimited joint and several liability, meaning each partner can be held responsible for the firm's entire debt.
  • Mutual Agency: Every partner is both an agent (represents others) and a principal (bound by others' acts).
  • Shared Control: Decisions are generally made through mutual consent and joint efforts.

docs.title: 2. Types of Partners
docs.text:
• Active: Contributes capital, manages the firm, and has unlimited liability.
  • Sleeping/Dormant: Contributes capital and shares profits but does not participate in management.
  • Secret: Association with the firm is unknown to the public; otherwise, functions like an active partner.
  • Nominal: Allows the use of their name; does not contribute capital or manage, but is liable to third parties.
  • Minor Partner: Cannot be a full partner but can be admitted to the benefits of the firm with consent. Their liability is limited to their capital contribution, and they do not manage the firm.

docs.title: 3. Merits and Limitations
docs.text:
• Merits: Easy formation/closure, balanced decision-making through specialization, more funds than a sole proprietor, and shared risk.
  • Limitations: Unlimited liability, potential for conflicts between partners, lack of business continuity, and low public confidence (as accounts are not public).

docs.title: IV. Joint Hindu Family Business (HUF)
docs.text: A unique Indian form of business owned and carried on by members of a Hindu Undivided Family.

docs.title: 1. Key Features
docs.text:
• Membership: Acquired by birth; three successive generations can be members (co-parceners).
  • Karta: The eldest male (or female per 2005 amendment) member who has absolute control and unlimited liability.
  • Liability of Members: Co-parceners (members other than Karta) have limited liability up to their share in the property.
  • Continuity: Stable; the death of the Karta does not end the business as the next eldest takes over.

docs.title: 2. Merits and Limitations
docs.text:
• Merits: Effective control by Karta, stability, and high loyalty among family members.
  • Limitations: Resources limited to ancestral property, Karta is overburdened with liability/management, and the decline of joint families affects this model.

docs.title: V. Joint Stock Company
docs.text: A voluntary association with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession, and a common seal. It is governed by The Companies Act, 2013.

docs.title: 1. Key Features
docs.text:
• Artificial Person: Created by law; it can own property and enter contracts but cannot breathe or talk.
  • Separate Legal Entity: Distinct from its owners (shareholders).
  • Perpetual Succession: "Members may come and go, but the company continues" until legally wound up.
  • Limited Liability: Shareholders are only liable up to the unpaid amount on their shares.
  • Management: Controlled by an elected Board of Directors.

docs.title: 2. Private vs. Public Companies
docs.text: Feature Private Limited Company Public Limited Company Members Min 2 / Max 200 Min 7 / Max Unlimited Share Transfer Restricted among members Freely transferable 24/7 Public Invitation Prohibited Allowed (Prospectus required) Directors Minimum 2 Minimum 3 Name Clause Must end with "Pvt Ltd" Must end with "Ltd"

docs.title: 3. Formation and Documents
docs.text:
Formation is a complex, expensive process involving regulators like SEBI and the Registrar of Companies (ROC).

  • Memorandum of Association (MOA): The fundamental document containing five clauses: Name, Location, Objective, Liability, and Capital.
  • Articles of Association (AOA): Internal rules for share transfer, voting, meetings, and director appointments.

Charateristics of company: 1. Huge capital 2. Stability of business 3. Economies of scale 4. Scope of expansion 5. Professional management 6. Tax benefits 7. Risk diffusion: (by large number of shareholders. They need to bear risk only up to the extent of amount of shares).

docs.title: VI. Cooperative Society
docs.text:
A voluntary association managed democratically for the benefit of its members to achieve common economic goals.

  • Governance: Managed by an elected committee.
  • Characteristics: Separate legal status, stable existence, and limited liability for members.
  • Example: Amul, which grew from a small group of farmers in 1946 to a massive network.

docs.title: VII. Anatomy of an Industrial Unit
docs.text:
An industrial unit is divided into four main quadrants surrounding Corporate Management (Planning, Organizing, Leading, Controlling):

  1. Finance: Budgeting, capital management, and accounting.
  2. Production: Plant maintenance, quality control, and safety.
  3. Personnel: Recruitment, training, and labor relations.
  4. Marketing: Demand forecasting, distribution, and advertising.

docs.title: RBI
docs.text: The following notes provide a comprehensive detailed overview of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), covering its history, structure, and functions as detailed in the source material.

docs.title: I. Historical Background of Banking in India
docs.text:
• Early Modern Banking: The first bank on modern lines was established in 1770 by a British Agency House. The Bank of Hindustan (1770) was the first Indian bank.
  • Presidency Banks: The East India Company established three Presidency banks: Bank of Bengal (1806), Bank of Bombay (1840), and Bank of Madras (1843), which were authorized to issue notes in their regions.
  • Expansion: Key milestones included the establishment of Allahabad Bank (1865) and the Oudh Commercial Bank (1881), which was the first limited liability bank managed by Indians. Punjab National Bank followed in 1894.
  • Imperial Bank of India: Formed in 1921 by amalgamating the three presidency banks, it performed some central banking functions until the RBI was established.
  • Post-Independence Status: By 1951, there were 566 private commercial banks, though bank deposits accounted for less than 1% of national income.

docs.title: II. Establishment and Purpose of the RBI
docs.text:
• Founding: The RBI was established on April 1, 1935, based on the recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission (Central Banking Enquiry Commission) and the RBI Act of 1934.
  • Capital Structure: It started with a share capital of Rs. 5 crores, initially owned by private shareholders in units of Rs. 100.
  • Apex Role: As the apex financial institution, it is entrusted with controlling, supervising, promoting, developing, and planning the financial system.
  • Preamble: Its basic functions are to regulate the issue of bank notes, keep reserves to secure monetary stability, and operate the currency and credit system to the country’s advantage.

docs.title: III. Management and Organization
docs.text: The RBI is governed by a Central Board of Directors appointed by the Government of India.

docs.title: 1. Central Board
docs.text:
• Consists of 20 members: A Governor (Chief Executive), 4 Deputy Governors, and 15 Directors (including 4 from local boards and 1 Finance Secretary).
  • Tenure: Governors and Deputy Governors serve up to 5 years; Directors serve 4 years with retirement by rotation.
  • Meetings: A Committee of the Central Board meets weekly (usually Wednesdays).

docs.title: 2. Local Boards
docs.text:
• Located in Mumbai (Western), Kolkata (Eastern), New Delhi (Northern), and Chennai (Southern).
  • Each board has 5 members appointed by the Central Government to advise on local matters and represent territorial/economic interests.

docs.title: 3. Specialized Departments
docs.text:
Main departments include:

  • Issue Department: Currency distribution.
  • Banking Department: Government transactions and commercial bank reserves.
  • Banking Development: Expanding facilities to rural/unbanked areas.
  • Banking Operations: Supervision and control of banking institutions.
  • Non-Banking Companies: Regulation of NBFCs.
  • Agricultural Credit / Industrial Finance: Sector-specific funding problems.
  • Exchange Control: Purchase and sale of foreign exchange.
  • Legal Department: Advising other departments.
  • Research and Statistics: Conducting research on money, credit, and finance.

docs.title: IV. Core Functions of the RBI
docs.text: The RBI's functions are classified into Monetary, Supervisory, and Promotional/Developmental.

docs.title: 1. Monetary (Central Banking) Functions
docs.text:
• Issue of Currency: Under Section 22, the RBI has the monopoly on note issue (except one-rupee notes and coins, which are issued by the Ministry of Finance).
    • Minimum Reserve System: Since 1956, the RBI must maintain a minimum reserve of gold or foreign securities (previously a 40% proportional reserve).
  • Banker to the Government: Acts as a banker, financial agent, and advisor to Central and State governments.
    • Services: Accepts deposits, makes payments, manages public debt, and sells Treasury Bills (91-day maturity).
    • Advances: Provides short-term advances (up to 3 months) without collateral.
  • Banker’s Bank: Maintains cash balances of scheduled banks and acts as the "lender of last resort" during financial crises.

docs.title: 2. Credit Control Measures
docs.text:
The RBI ensures price stability and economic growth through two types of controls:

A. Quantitative Measures (Volume of Credit):

  • Bank Rate: The rate at which RBI lends to banks without security. Raising it reduces the money supply to curb inflation.
  • Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): The percentage of deposits banks must keep with the RBI. Increasing CRR reduces the money supply.
  • Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): The percentage of reserves banks must maintain in liquid assets like gold or government securities.
  • Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF): Includes Repo (banks borrow from RBI) and Reverse Repo (banks park funds with RBI).
  • Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): Allows banks to borrow overnight funds by dipping into their SLR portfolio.
  • Open Market Operations (OMO): Buying bonds to increase money supply (expansionary) or selling bonds to reduce it (contractionary).

B. Qualitative Measures (Direction of Credit):

  • Moral Suasion: Requesting banks to follow specific actions, like avoiding unproductive loans.
  • Credit Ceiling: Setting limits on loans to commercial banks.
  • Credit Authorization Scheme: Requiring prior RBI approval for large fresh credits.
  • Regulation of Margin Requirements: Fixing the difference between the loan amount and the value of collateral to influence borrowing in specific sectors (e.g., agriculture).

docs.title: 3. Foreign Exchange Management
docs.text:
• Set up the Exchange Control Department (1939) to regulate business.
  • Custodian: Acts as the custodian of foreign exchange reserves (Euro, USD, Yen, etc.) and maintains the external value of the Rupee.

docs.title: 4. Supervisory Functions
docs.text: • Relates to licensing, branch expansion, liquidity of assets, amalgamation, and liquidation of commercial and cooperative banks.

docs.title: 5. Promotional and Developmental Functions
docs.text:
• Agricultural Credit: Managed through the Agricultural Credit Department and two specific funds (Long-term operations and Stabilization funds).
  • Industrial Finance: Helped establish public sector corporations like IFCI, SFC, IDBI, IRCI, and UTI to provide short, medium, and long-term finance.

docs.title: Question 1: Evaluation of Cancer Detection ML System
docs.text:
1.1 Given - Total population = 100,000 - Actual cancer patients (positive class) = 400 - Healthy individuals (negative class) = 99,600 - Correctly identified cancer patients = 100 - Healthy individuals incorrectly flagged as cancer = 200 - Total wrong predictions = 500

  1. TP -> Correct Prediction + Predicted as has Cancer => Patients who have cancer and predicted as has cancer. => 100
  2. FP -> Incorrect Prediction + Predicted as has Cancer => Patients who are healthy and predicted as has cancer. => 200
  3. TN -> Correct Prediction + Predicted as has no Cancer => Patients who are healthy and predicted as healthy. => 100,000 - 400 - 200 = 99,400
  4. FN -> Incorrect Prediction + Predicted as has no Cancer => Patients who has cancer but predicted as has no cancer. => 300

1.2. Clinically more dangerous error

False Negatives are more dangerous than False Positives.

Justification:

  • A false negative means cancer is not detected, which can delay diagnosis and treatment.
  • Delayed treatment in cancer can significantly reduce survival rates.
  • False positives cause stress and additional tests, but usually do not threaten life directly.

1.3. $\(Accuracy = \frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}\)$ $\(Accuracy = \frac{100+99,400}{100+200+99,400+300}=99.5\%\)$

  • Why deceptively high? Because the dataset is highly imbalanced. Even if the model predicted everyone was "Healthy," it would still achieve 99.6% accuracy

1.4. $\(Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{100}{100 + 200} = 33.3\%\)$ - Only 1/3 of people flagged with cancer actually have it. Trustworthiness is low

1.5. $\(Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{100}{100+300} = 25\%\)$ - The system misses 75% of actual cancer cases, making it very ineffective for screening

1.6. - Accuracy is high because it is dominated by the massive number of True Negatives (healthy people). Recall is low because the model fails to identify the majority of the small "positive" class

1.7. - Recall is the most useful metric here. In medical screening, the priority is to ensure no actual cases are missed (minimizing False Negatives), even if it means more follow-up tests for False Positives

1.8. - Benefit: The F1-score provides a single harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, penalizing the model for having a very low value in either. - Insufficiency: F1 treats Precision and Recall as equally important. In this clinical case, Recall is far more critical than Precision, so F1 might still mask a dangerously low Recall rate

docs.title: Question 2: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
docs.text:
2.1 - Query point: Q = (3, 3) - Distance metric: Squared Euclidean Distance

Point ID x y Class Distance Calculation \(d^2\) A1 1 1 A \((3-1)^2 + (3-1)^2\) 8 A2 1 3 A \((3-1)^2 + (3-3)^2\) 4 A3 2 2 A \((3-2)^2 + (3-2)^2\) 2 B1 4 4 B \((3-4)^2 + (3-4)^2\) 2 B2 5 4 B \((3-5)^2 + (3-4)^2\) 5 B3 4 5 B \((3-4)^2 + (3-5)^2\) 5

2.2. - when k = 1 - Nearest points are A3 or B1 - Votes for A = 1 - Votes for B = 1 - There is a tie, so we choose the first one => A - Prediction = A (tie breaked) - when k = 3 - Nearest points are A3, B1, A2 - Votes for A = 2 - Votes for B = 1 - Prediction = A - when k = 5 - Nearest points are A3, B1, A2, B2, B3 - Votes for A = 2 - Votes for B = 3 - Prediction = B

2.3. - A very large k includes points that are far away and likely belong to different clusters. This ignores the local structure of the data and makes the decision boundary too smooth, essentially predicting the majority class of the entire dataset regardless of where the query point is located.

2.4. k = 1 is more affected.

  • Why: k = 1 makes its decision based solely on the single nearest neighbor. If that one point is mislabeled, the prediction will be 100% wrong. k = 5 is more robust because it averages the votes of 5 points, so one bad point is less likely to flip the final result.

2.5. - a) Greatest Contributor: The neighbors with the smallest distance (A3 and B1) contribute the most. - b) Reducing Ties: Yes. Weighted voting makes it much rarer for the sums of weights to be exactly equal, as it accounts for the precise proximity of each point rather than just a simple count.

docs.title: 2.1 Target Function
docs.text: In this problem, we aim to predict a student’s Exam Score using two independent variables: Study Hours and Sleep Hours.

docs.title: Mathematical Model
docs.text: \[y = w_1 \cdot x_1 + w_2 \cdot x_2 + b\]

docs.title: Variable Definitions
docs.text:
• y: Exam Score (dependent variable)
  • \(x_1\): Study Hours (independent variable)
  • \(x_2\): Sleep Hours (independent variable)
  • \(w_1\): Weight associated with Study Hours
  • \(w_2\): Weight associated with Sleep Hours

1. Identical Predictions Both the scaled and unscaled models predict an exam score of 77.0 for the input (3, 7). Feature scaling does not change the final prediction for linear regression.
  2. Different Coefficient Values The numerical values of the coefficients change because feature scaling standardizes the input features to a common range.
  3. Why Feature Scaling Matters
    • Improves numerical stability during optimization

    • Makes coefficients easier to compare
    • Prevents features with larger magnitudes from dominating the model

docs.title: 3.2 Model Comparison
docs.text:
Three different models were trained and compared: Linear, Polynomial (Degree 2), and Polynomial (Degree 4).

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.array([1, 5, 10, 18, 30])

def train_linear(x, y):
    model = LinearRegression()
    model.fit(x, y)
    return model, model.predict(x)

def train_polynomial(x, y, degree):
    features = PolynomialFeatures(degree=degree)
    x_poly = features.fit_transform(x)
    model = LinearRegression()
    model.fit(x_poly, y)
    return model, features, model.predict(x_poly)

def compute_cost(y_true, y_pred):
    return np.mean((y_pred - y_true) ** 2) / 2

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
plt.scatter(x, y, color='navy', s=120, edgecolors='black', label='Actual Data Points')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('Scatter Plot: x vs y')
plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
plt.legend()
plt.show()

linear_model, y_pred_linear = train_linear(x, y)
print(f"\nLinear function: y = {linear_model.coef_[0]:.2f}*x + {linear_model.intercept_:.2f}\n")

poly2_model, poly2_features, y_pred_poly2 = train_polynomial(x, y, 2)
a0 = poly2_model.intercept_
a1, a2 = poly2_model.coef_[1:3]
print("Polynomial function (degree = 2):")
print(f"y = {a2:.3f}x^2 + {a1:.3f}x + {a0:.3f}\n")

poly4_model, poly4_features, y_pred_poly4 = train_polynomial(x, y, 4)
a0 = poly4_model.intercept_
a1, a2, a3, a4 = poly4_model.coef_[1:5]
print("Polynomial function (degree = 4):")
print(f"y = {a4:.3f}x^4 + {a3:.3f}x^3 + {a2:.3f}x^2 + {a1:.3f}x + {a0:.3f}")

cost_linear = compute_cost(y, y_pred_linear)
cost_poly2 = compute_cost(y, y_pred_poly2)
cost_poly4 = compute_cost(y, y_pred_poly4)

print(f"\nLinear Model Cost: {cost_linear:.4f}")
print(f"Polynomial (Degree 2) Model Cost: {cost_poly2:.4f}")
print(f"Polynomial (Degree 4) Model Cost: {cost_poly4:.4f}\n")

x_line = np.linspace(1, 5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.scatter(x, y, color='navy', s=120, edgecolors='black', label='Actual Data')
plt.plot(x_line, linear_model.predict(x_line), 'r--', linewidth=2, label='Linear Model')
plt.plot(x_line, poly2_model.predict(poly2_features.transform(x_line)), 'g-', linewidth=2, label='Polynomial (Degree 2)')
plt.plot(x_line, poly4_model.predict(poly4_features.transform(x_line)), 'p:', linewidth=3, label='Polynomial (Degree 4)')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('Linear vs Polynomial Regression')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
models = ['Linear', 'Polynomial (Deg 2)', 'Polynomial (Deg 4)']
costs = [cost_linear, cost_poly2, cost_poly4]
bars = plt.bar(models, costs, color=['green', 'purple', 'blue'])
plt.ylabel('Cost (MSE / 2)')
plt.title('Model Cost Comparison')
plt.grid(True, axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

for bar in bars:
    plt.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, bar.get_height(), f'{bar.get_height():.3f}', ha='center', va='bottom')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

test_points = np.array([[2.5], [3.5], [4.5]])

pred_linear = linear_model.predict(test_points)
pred_poly2 = poly2_model.predict(poly2_features.transform(test_points))
pred_poly4 = poly4_model.predict(poly4_features.transform(test_points))

print("Predictions:")
for i, val in enumerate(test_points):
    print(f"x = {val[0]}: Linear = {pred_linear[i]:.2f}, Polynomial(2) = {pred_poly2[i]:.2f}, Polynomial(4) = {pred_poly4[i]:.2f}")

docs.title: 3.4 Model overfitting, underfitting
docs.text:
Based on the analysis:

  • Best Model: Polynomial Regression (Degree 2)
    • Captures the quadratic relationship effectively
    • Achieves very low training error
    • Maintains a good balance between bias and variance
    • Avoids unnecessary complexity

docs.title: Logistic Regression, Regularization and Bias Variance
1. The Bias-Variance Shift
docs.text:
By applying heavy L2 regularization, you essentially traded High Variance for High Bias.

  • Initial State: The model was over-complex (High Variance), memorizing the training data perfectly but failing to generalize to new patients.
  • The Shift: The L2 penalty reduced model complexity by shrinking the weights. However, the penalty was too "heavy," pushing the model past the sweet spot into underfitting (High Bias). It became too simple to see the patterns of the rare disease.

docs.title: 2. The Sigmoid "Flattening"
docs.text:
The sigmoid function is defined as:

$$ \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(wx + b)}} $$ - Flattening: When L2 forces weights (\(w\)) to be very small, the input \(z\) stays near zero. This creates a flatter, less responsive curve rather than a sharp "S" shape. - The Problem: A flatter curve means the model is less sensitive to changes in patient data. Because the disease is so rare, a flat curve makes it nearly impossible for the output probability to "climb" high enough to cross the 0.5 threshold to predict "Sick."

docs.title: 3. The Accuracy Paradox
docs.text:
In a dataset where 99.5% of people are healthy, accuracy is a trap.

  • The Default Score: If your model simply predicts "Healthy" for every single person, it achieves 99.5% accuracy while doing zero actual work.
  • Why it's useless: A doctor doesn't need a model to tell them a healthy person is healthy; they need it to find the needle in the haystack. By "improving" accuracy, you likely just trained the model to ignore the 0.5% of sick patients to avoid the risk of being "wrong" on the majority.

docs.title: 4. Critical Decision
docs.text:
I would choose Model A.

  • Clinical Priorities: In medicine, a False Negative (missing a sick patient) is far more dangerous than a False Positive (a "scare" for a healthy person).
  • The Choice: Model A has a high Recall, catching 95% of cases. Even though it "over-diagnoses" (False Positives), those patients can be cleared with follow-up testing. Model B is "accurate" but lethal, as it leaves 90% of sick patients untreated (False Negatives).

docs.title: 1. Prior Probabilities
docs.text:

Total number of messages:

Number of Ham messages:

docs.title: 5. Why Smoothing Matters
docs.text: Laplace smoothing prevents the Zero Probability Problem. Without smoothing, if a feature value never appears in a class (for example, meeting in Spam), the probability becomes zero. When probabilities are multiplied together, one zero causes the entire class probability to become zero, making comparison between classes impossible.

docs.title: 3. Why Bagging + Voting Improves Performance
docs.text: Combining multiple weak learners into an ensemble reduces overall variance (overfitting). Since each tree is trained on a different bootstrap sample, they make different errors. Voting allows these errors to cancel out, leading to a more robust model.

docs.title: 4. Random Forest vs Bagging
docs.text:
• Bagging: Randomizes the data samples.
  • Random Forest: Randomizes both data samples and feature selection during splits.

This makes trees less correlated and improves overall performance.

docs.title: Data Exploration
docs.text: Detailed below are the comprehensive notes derived from the Data Exploration source material, covering the objectives, processes, data types, and remediation techniques.

docs.title: 1. Core Objective and Process Overview
docs.text:
The primary goal of data exploration is to understand the relationships between a dataset's elements and the overall data spread. It is the initial step in the machine learning process.

The Detailed Machine Learning Process:

  1. Step 1: Preparing to Model – Includes inputting data and performing exploration.
  2. Step 2: Learning – Applying algorithms to the refined data.
  3. Step 3: Performance Evaluation – Assessing how well the model learned.
  4. Step 4: Performance Improvement – Refining the model for better results.

docs.title: 2. The First Step: Data Exploration
docs.text:
Every machine learning activity starts with data. The nature of exploration depends on the type of learning:

  • Supervised Learning: Exploration involves labeled training data followed by unlabeled test data.
  • Unsupervised Learning: There is no labeled data; the task is to find inherent patterns within the input.

Key Exploration Goals:

  • Understand the type and quality of the data.
  • Analyze the relationships between different data elements (inter-feature relationships).
  • Identify potential issues to determine necessary pre-processing activities.

docs.title: 3. Data Preparation and Remediation
docs.text:
Once data is input, several typical preparation activities occur:

  • Identify Data Types: Distinguishing between numeric and categorical attributes.
  • Quality Assessment: Finding potential issues like outliers or missing values.
  • Remediation:
    • Handling Outliers: These abnormally high or low values impact prediction accuracy, particularly in regression. Approaches include:
      • Removal: Deleting the outlier records if they are few.
      • Imputation: Replacing outliers with the mean, median, or mode.
      • Capping: Replacing values that fall outside 1.5 times the Interquartile Range (IQR).
    • Handling Missing Values: Caused by surveyor omission or responder error. Methods include:
      • Elimination: Deleting records with missing data.
      • Imputation: Assigning the most frequent value, such as the mean, median, or mode.
      • Estimation: Planting values from similar data points into the missing slots.

docs.title: 4. Detailed Classification of Data Types
docs.text: Data is broadly divided into two categories, each requiring a different exploration approach:

docs.title: A. Qualitative (Categorical) Data
docs.text:
This provides non-measurable information about the quality of an object.

  • Nominal Data: Named values with no numeric value or quantification (e.g., car names).
  • Ordinal Data: Categorical data that implies a specific order (e.g., performance ranked as "Good," "Average," or "Poor").

docs.title: B. Quantitative (Numeric) Data
docs.text:
Measurable data used for mathematical calculations.

  • Discrete Attributes: Assumes a finite or countably infinite number of values (e.g., roll numbers, number of cylinders, model year).
  • Continuous Attributes: Can assume any possible real number value (e.g., length, weight, price, horsepower).

docs.title: Central Tendency
docs.text:
• Mean: The average value, calculated from the cumulative sum of all elements. It is highly sensitive to outliers, which can drastically shift its value.
  • Median: The central data value when arranged in order. It is less impacted by extreme values than the mean.
  • Significance: A high deviation between the mean and median suggests outliers that require investigation and potential remediation.

docs.title: Measuring Data Spread (Dispersion)
docs.text:
Any numerical attribute can be summarized by five values: Minimum, First Quartile (Q1), Median (Q2), Third Quartile (Q3), and Maximum.

  • Box Plot: A visual representation of this five-number summary.
    • Advantages: Organizes large amounts of data and effectively visualizes outliers.
    • Disadvantages: Not suitable for detailed distribution analysis because it only provides a summary.
  • Histogram: A plot used to understand the distribution of numeric data across a series of intervals.

docs.title: 6. Exploring Relationships Between Variables
docs.text:
• Scatter Plot: Used to visualize bivariate relationships (relationships between two variables). Dots are drawn on coordinates (x, y) to show how one attribute changes in relation to another (e.g., displacement vs. mpg).
  • Two-Way Cross-Tabulations (Contingency Tables): A matrix format used to concisely summarize the relationship and frequency distribution between two categorical attributes.

docs.title: 7. Advanced Exploration Techniques
docs.text:
• Dimensionality Reduction: Reducing the number of features to save computational time and space. It helps eliminate redundancy and makes models easier to understand. Popular techniques include PCA, SVD, and LDA.
  • Feature Engineering: The critical process of translating a dataset into features that represent patterns more effectively to improve learning performance. It involves three components:
    1. Feature Construction.
    2. Feature Selection.
    3. Feature Transformation.

docs.title: 8. Dimensionality Reduction
docs.text:
• Dimensionality reduction helps in reducing irrelevance and redundancy in features. Also, it is easier to understand a model if the number of features involved in the learning activity is less
  • Techniques are:
    1. PCA
    2. SVD
    3. LDA

docs.text: $$ w = w - \alpha\frac{\partial J(w, b)}{\partial w} $$ $$ b = b - \alpha\frac{\partial J(w, b)}{\partial b} $$ - \(\alpha\) is the learning rate $\(f(x) = wx + b\)$ - when the number of features is >= 2, wx becomes dot product

docs.title: Regression Metrics
docs.text:

  • MAE $$ J(w, b) = \frac{1}{n}\Sigma{|f(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}|} $$
