A secure system should authenticate sensor messages and validate their values before using them in control logic.

docs.title: Q16. How is your project related to STUXNET?
docs.text:
STUXNET demonstrated how cyberattacks could manipulate industrial control systems and affect physical processes.

My project simulates a PLC-based industrial environment and demonstrates how unauthorized commands, IP spoofing, invalid authentication, and replay attacks could interfere with actuator control.

It is a simplified educational model of industrial cybersecurity threats, not a reproduction of STUXNET.

docs.title: 23. How I would explain the entire project to the faculty
docs.text:
If your faculty asks, "Explain your project and what exactly you have implemented," I'd structure your explanation like this:

  1. We created an IIoT environment using ns-3 with four nodes: a temperature sensor, PLC, cooler actuator, and attacker.
  2. All nodes are connected through a CSMA-based LAN and communicate using IPv4 and UDP.
  3. We implemented a lightweight CoAP message encoder and decoder rather than relying on an external CoAP library.
  4. The sensor periodically sends temperature readings to the PLC using CoAP POST requests.
  5. The PLC processes the measurements and sends commands to the cooler depending on a predefined temperature threshold.
  6. We introduced an attacker that can monitor network communication using promiscuous packet capture.
  7. We implemented direct command injection, IP spoofing, invalid-HMAC attacks, and replay attacks.
  8. We introduced security mechanisms including IP-based filtering, HMAC authentication, and sequence-number-based replay protection.
  9. Finally, we use different configuration combinations to evaluate whether the defenses successfully prevent unauthorized control commands.

That is a solid explanation of the project.

docs.title: 24. My recommendation: Understand these five things particularly well
docs.text:
If I were examining this project, these are the five areas I'd spend the most time questioning you about:

Priority Topic Why 1 CoAP packet structure and communication You implemented the protocol yourself 2 Raw sockets and IP spoofing Your attacker manually constructs IP packets 3 Promiscuous mode and packet sniffing Important networking concept 4 HMAC and replay protection Central to your security implementation 5 PLC control logic and STUXNET Central to the assignment's objective

You already know C++ and networking fundamentals, so I wouldn't spend too much time revising basic syntax. Focus on how the different protocol layers interact.

docs.title: One thing I'd like to examine next
docs.text:
We've understood the attacker and network construction, but there's one missing piece needed to explain the security implementation with complete accuracy: the Cooler and PLC code.

In particular, I'd like to trace:

  • Exactly how the Cooler validates the source IP.
  • How it extracts and verifies the HMAC.
  • How it maintains the last accepted sequence number.
  • In what order it performs the security checks.
  • How the PLC generates the HMAC and sequence number.
  • How the PLC decides when to turn the cooler ON or OFF.

Share Cooler.cc, PLC.cc, and, if possible, the HMAC utility implementation. Then we can trace a legitimate command and each of the four attacks line by line, including exactly which defense rejects each packet.

docs.title: 2.1 Version (2 bits)
docs.text:
Identifies the CoAP protocol version.

Currently, the standardized CoAP version is:

Version = 1

It occupies the first two bits of the first byte.

docs.title: 2.2 Type (2 bits)
docs.text:
Specifies the message type.

CoAP defines four message types:

Type Value Meaning CON 0 Confirmable NON 1 Non-confirmable ACK 2 Acknowledgement RST 3 Reset

These are important because they determine how CoAP handles message delivery.

docs.title: CON — Confirmable
docs.text:
A confirmable message requires acknowledgement.

Suppose a PLC receives a command to activate a critical actuator.

The sender wants to know whether the message was successfully received.

It sends:

Client → Server: CON POST /command

The receiver responds:

Server → Client: ACK

If the sender doesn't receive an acknowledgement within the retransmission timeout, it can retransmit the message.

docs.title: NON — Non-confirmable
docs.text:
A non-confirmable message does not require an acknowledgement.

Useful for frequently transmitted sensor measurements where occasional packet loss is acceptable.

For example:

Sensor → PLC: NON POST /temperature

If one temperature reading gets lost, the next reading may arrive shortly afterward.

docs.title: ACK — Acknowledgement
docs.text:
Indicates that a confirmable message was received.

An ACK can be:

  • An empty ACK, which acknowledges receipt but does not contain the response.
  • A piggybacked ACK, which acknowledges the request and carries the response in the same message.

Your implementation uses the second approach.

docs.title: RST — Reset
docs.text:
Indicates that a message was received but could not be processed or associated with the expected communication context.

For example, a device might receive a message with an unknown Message ID and respond with RST.

docs.title: 2.3 Token Length (4 bits)
docs.text:
Abbreviated as TKL.

Specifies the length of the Token field.

Valid values:

0 to 8 bytes

Why do we need a token?

The Message ID and Token serve different purposes.

  • Message ID: Identifies a CoAP message for message-layer reliability and duplicate detection. Each message will be having a new message id. It will be sequential
  • Token: Correlates a response with the corresponding request. Is for identifying which response map to which request. A request and response will have the same token. Token of request is chosen randomly.

2 cases: - Client or server is free: Might send piggy backed response which will contain type = ACK and the response payload also. In this case, message id will be the same - Client or server is busy: Might send a empty ACK so that other guy will not re-transmit. In this case, the message id will be different

For example:

Request:
Message ID = 100
Token      = 0x12 0x34

Response:
Message ID = 100
Token      = 0x12 0x34

For a piggybacked ACK, the Message ID is copied from the request.

For a separate response, the response has its own Message ID, but retains the original request's Token.

This distinction is important.

docs.title: 2.4 Code (8 bits)
docs.text:
Specifies the request method or response status.

It is divided into three bits for the class and five bits for the detail.

The general representation is:

Class.Detail

docs.title: Request codes
docs.text:
Method Code Meaning GET 0.01 Retrieve a resource POST 0.02 Create a resource or process submitted data PUT 0.03 Update or create a resource DELETE 0.04 Delete a resource

For example:

0.02 = POST

Your implementation uses POST.

docs.title: Response codes
docs.text:
Some commonly used response codes:

Code Meaning 2.01 Created 2.02 Deleted 2.04 Changed 2.05 Content 4.00 Bad Request 4.01 Unauthorized 4.03 Forbidden 4.04 Not Found 5.00 Internal Server Error

An interesting detail for your project:

Your earlier implementation uses response code 131.

In hexadecimal:

131 decimal = 0x83

Breaking it down:

10000011

Class = 100 = 4

Detail = 00011 = 3

Therefore:

4.03 = Forbidden

This is appropriate when your PLC rejects an unauthorized command.

docs.title: 2.5 Message ID (16 bits)
docs.text:
The Message ID is a 16-bit identifier.

Its range is:

0 to 65535

It serves two major purposes:

  1. Detecting duplicate messages.
  2. Matching acknowledgements with confirmable messages.

For example:

Request:
Message ID = 500

ACK:
Message ID = 500

If a confirmable request is retransmitted because its ACK was lost, the receiver can recognize the duplicate using the Message ID.

Note that Message IDs are scoped to the message-layer communication between endpoints and are not globally unique identifiers.

docs.title: 2.6 Token (0–8 bytes)
docs.text:
As explained earlier, the Token correlates requests and responses.

Unlike the Message ID, it belongs to the request-response interaction.

For example:

Request:
Token = AB CD

Response:
Token = AB CD

A server can use the token to identify which request a response belongs to.

Your implementation generates a two-byte token from the Message ID. That is a convenient choice for your simulation, although a production implementation should generate tokens with appropriate uniqueness.

docs.title: 2.7 Options
docs.text:
Options provide additional metadata about a CoAP message.

Examples include:

Option Option Number Purpose If-Match 1 Conditional request Uri-Host 3 Host identification ETag 4 Resource version identification If-None-Match 5 Conditional request Observe 6 Resource observation Uri-Port 7 Port information Location-Path 8 Resource location Uri-Path 11 Resource path Content-Format 12 Payload format Max-Age 14 Response freshness Uri-Query 15 Query parameters Accept 17 Accepted response format Block2 23 Block-wise transfer Block1 27 Block-wise transfer

Your implementation currently supports only the URI-Path option.

docs.title: How are options encoded?
docs.text:
This is an interesting part of CoAP.

Each option has:

+-------------------+
| Delta | Length    |
+-------------------+
| Option Value      |
+-------------------+

Both Delta and Length are four bits.

Delta is the difference between the current option number and the previous option number.

Length specifies the number of bytes in the option value.

Why Delta instead of storing the complete option number?

Because CoAP options are ordered by option number. Delta encoding reduces the number of bits required.

For the first option:

Previous option number = 0
Current option number  = 11 (URI-Path)

Delta = 11 - 0 = 11

Suppose the URI path is:

/temperature

The option header is:

Delta  = 11
Length = 11

Assuming the path segment is temperature, which has 11 characters:

Option Header = 1011 1011
              = 0xBB

The complete option becomes:

BB 74 65 6D 70 65 72 61 74 75 72 65

Here:

  • BB is the option header.
  • Remaining bytes represent temperature in ASCII.

One subtlety: URI-Path is a repeatable option. A path such as /sensor/temperature is encoded using two URI-Path options, one for sensor and another for temperature.

docs.title: 2.8 Payload
docs.text:
The payload contains the actual application data.

For example:

POST /temperature

Payload: 75

The payload is optional.

CoAP uses a special byte:

0xFF

to indicate the beginning of the payload.

Therefore:

Options
0xFF
Payload

If the message has no payload, the payload marker must not be included.

docs.title: CoAP
docs.text:
• Constraint Application Protocol
  • uses UDP
  • Port 5683
  • Application layer protocol

Why UDP? 1. No connection establishment overhead. 2. Smaller communication overhead. 3. Less resource consumption. 4. Suitable for constrained devices.

UDP means, no reliability, no ordering, no duplicate protection

Methods 1. GET 2. POST 3. PUT 4. DELETE

docs.title: BGP
docs.text:
• Works in application layer
  • Path vector routing protocol
  • Uses TCP
  • port 179
  • When BGP is used to exchange routes within the same Autonomous System, it is called iBGP (Internal BGP).
  • BGP between different Autonomous Systems is called eBGP (External BGP).

docs.title: What is an AS?
docs.text:
• An Autonomous System (AS) is a group of IP networks and routers managed under a common routing policy.
  • An AS is identified by an Autonomous System Number (ASN).

docs.title: How BGP works?
docs.text:
• First it establishes a TCP connection
  • Then they exchange OPEN messages
    • It contains: BGP version, sender AS number, hold time, BGP identifier, optional capabilities.
    • If the required parameters are compatible, the peers establish a BGP session
  • Sends KEEPALIVE messages in regular intervals to keep the BGP session alive
  • Exchange routers using UPDATE messages
  • Receiving routers evaluates the route. It checks
    • Whether the route passes its import policies and filters.
    • Whether the route is valid and usable.
    • Whether its next hop is reachable.
    • Whether a different route is preferred according to BGP's decision process.
  • The route is advertised to other BGP peers when permitted

docs.title: BGP message types
docs.text:
Message Purpose Easy way to remember OPEN Establishes BGP session parameters Start the conversation KEEPALIVE Maintains the session Are we still connected? UPDATE Advertises routes or withdraws routes Here is a route change NOTIFICATION Reports an error or a session-ending condition Something went wrong ## BGP Attributes

AS_PATH - Records the AS a route has traversed - A path will be rejected if the AS sees its own ASN in the path LOCAL_PREF - helps an AS choose which exit path to prefer for outgoing traffic. - If there are multiple outgoing interfaces for a company, then the one with higher LOCAL_PREF will be taken MED - Multi-Exit Discriminator - It suggests other ASs which of the multiple entry points into an AS should be preferred for incoming traffic - Lower MED value is preferred NEXT_HOP - Identifies the next hop IP address associated with a BGP route ORIGIN - Indicates the origin category associated with a route in BGP. - Values can be IGP, EGP and INCOMPLETE - Preference IGP > EGP > INCOMPLETE Communities - Values attached to routes so that operators can classify routes and apply policies to them.

Attribute Main purpose Typical preference or use AS_PATH Records ASes traversed; helps prevent loops Shorter often preferred, all else equal LOCAL_PREF Chooses preferred exit path within an AS Higher preferred MED Suggests a preferred entry point to a neighboring AS Lower often preferred NEXT_HOP Identifies the next-hop IP Must be resolvable for the route to be usable ORIGIN Describes the route's origin category IGP, then EGP, then INCOMPLETE in traditional comparison COMMUNITY Tags routes for policy Depends on configured policy

docs.title: OSPF
docs.text:
• Link State Routing
  • Works in network layer (layer 3)
  • Uses IP protocol 89.
  • No transport layer
  • OSPF itself has transport layer features inbuilt
  • Since there is no transport layer, it has no port number
  • Multicast address:
    • 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers)
    • 224.0.0.6 (designated routers)

docs.title: How OSPF works
docs.text:
• Routers will periodically send Hello Packets to its configured neighbors
    • It will contain the hello interval, dead interval, router id, area id, authentication, subnet mask, priority, DR, BDR, neighbors etc
    • neighbors here means the list of routers to whom the router got a hello and became a neighbor
    • There are neighbors and adjacencies
    • Neighbors means, the routers have send eachother hello packets and established OSPF neighbor communication
    • Adjacency means, the routers have synchronized their link state database also.
  • Once router B becomes a neighbor, of router A, and vice versa, they starts sending DBB packets. Which will contain the data base description like which all router's topology he knows and how new is that entry.
  • Once the DBD is shared, the routers start sending LSR. Which is Link state request. It will request for missing or new LSAs.
  • For these LSR's, the routers respond with LSUs, which are Link State Updates which will contain LSAs which are Link State Advertisements.
  • For these LSU's the router sends back LSAck as acknowledgements.

If its a broadcast network, sending all these routing information to all routers in all combinations is not efficient. - So they will elect a DR and BDR which are Designated Router and Backup Designated Router. - The routers will establish the adjacencies with the DR instead of establishing it with all other routers. - Hello packets are send to discover one another even though DR is there - BDR takes over if DR fails - DR is elected based on priority value and on tie, it will take the router with higher router ID When a link fails, the router updates its local topology information and sends a LSA describing the change. The LSA is distributed through OSPF flooding process. During this LSA flooding process, that particular interface goes to DOWN state whereas all other pair of routers remain in their existing state.

docs.title: States in OSPF
docs.text:
• DOWN \= No hello packet have received from the neighbor
  • INIT \= Hello packet received the router but my router ID is not in the neighbour list in the Hello Packet
  • 2-WAY \= Bi directional communication is established when the routers see its own router ID in the neighbours Hello packet. In multi access networks, DR and BDR elections happens now.
  • EXSTART \= Master and slave roles are decided to manage the exchange of DBD
  • EXCHANGE \= Routers start exchanging DBD packets with the sequence number set by the master
  • LOADING \= Routers send LSR and LSU to synchronise their LSDBs
  • FULL \= LSDB is synchronised for both routers. Adjacency achieved

docs.text: LSA type Name General purpose Type 1 Router LSA Describes a router's links and local topology within an area Type 2 Network LSA Describes a multiaccess network and its attached routers; originated by the DR Type 3 Summary LSA Advertises inter-area network reachability Type 4 ASBR Summary LSA Provides information about how to reach an Autonomous System Boundary Router Type 5 AS-External LSA Advertises external routes redistributed into OSPF

docs.title: Network Types
docs.text:
Point to Point - direct communication link is present between exactly two devices - Link is dedicated to communication between the 2 devices - No other devices share the link Device A -------- Device B

Point to multi point - Connects one central device to multiple other devices - All other devices are connected to the central device

Multi access network - Multiple devices connect to and communicate over the same shared network segment or medium - Eg: An Ethernet LAN connecting multiple routers or computers through a switch

docs.title: OSPF Area
docs.text:
• A logical grouping of OSPF interfaces and routers.
  • Areas help OSPF scale to larger network by limiting the scope of detailed topology information and reducing routing overhead
  • Area 0 is called backbone area
  • In a conventional multiarea OSPF design, other areas connect to the backbone through Area Border Routers (ABR)
  • An ABR connects multiple OSPF areas and distributes the inter-area routing information
  • Within an area, routers maintain the area's link-state database and calculate intra-area routes
  • Between areas, OSPF can advertise reachability information without requiring every router to have the complete detailed topology of every other area.
  • This reduces the amount of topology information that needs to be maintained across the entire routing domain

docs.title: Router Roles
docs.text: Router role Meaning Internal Router All its OSPF interfaces belong to the same area Backbone Router Has an interface in Area 0 Area Border Router (ABR) Connects multiple OSPF areas Autonomous System Boundary Router (ASBR) Redistributes routing information from another source into OSPF

docs.title: RIP
docs.text:
• Distance vector routing
  • Is an transport layer protocol (sometimes said as "works in application layer")
  • Uses UDP in transport layer
  • Works for IPv4 and IPv6
  • RIPv1 and RIPv3 uses port 520 for IPv4 routing
  • RIPng uses port 521. Used for IPv6
  • No encryption
  • For security we can use authentication with plain text or MD5
  • Metric 16 means unreachable
  • A RIP response can contain upto 25 routes each 20 bytes
  • RIP header is 4 bytes
  • Total 4 + 20 * 25 = 504 bytes
  • Multicast address:
    • 224.0.0.9
    • FF02::9

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Admin configures the interfaces which RIP should work.
  • Every 30 seconds each routers sends its current routing information to its neighbouring routers.
  • Receiving this scheduled response will not trigger another response.
  • If a link goes down or up, it will trigger an update. It will send the new routing information to the neighbouring routers. Triggered update don't wait for 30 second interval.
  • When a router starts up it may send a RIP request asking its neighbours for routing information. Neighbours can reply with a RIP response containing all or part of its routing table.

Split Horizon - Routers generally don't advertise a route back out through the interface on which it learned that route Route poisoning - Advertising a failed destination with metric 16 so neighbouring routers know it is no longer reachable through that route.
